speechtext:
The House resumed from Friday, April 30, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance), that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. R. J. Manion.
Mr. GEORGE W. McPHEE (Yorkton) [DOT] Mr. Speaker, the debate was adjourned by the hon. member for L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Seguin) and I did not expect to be called upon at this early hour in the afternoon. However, before discussing the matter which is now engaging the attention of the House, namely the budget and the amendment, permit me to offer a few observations with regard to an address delivered in this House last Tuesday evening by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards). The manner in which the words were used would leave no doubt in our minds that the hon. gentleman expected a reply. Lest there be some misunderstanding with regard to what the hon. gentleman stated, let me read into my address the record of what was said by the hon. member:
Mr. Edwards (Frontenac): My hon. friends should not say "hear, hear", because if they were at all generous they must have recognized the fact that a large part of my time was taken up in what I believe was a fruitless effort in trying to force some common sense into heads which, so far as we have been able to judge, have shown no sign of possessing that desirable quality. I have not much hope that what I have said, and the instructions I have given, will have any effect, because you have to plant seed in fertile ground if it is to produce anything, and there is no fertility over yonder; there are no brains to furnish the necessary soil to produce results. I can only leave the matter with them, hoping against hope that Providence, which has done so much for the Liberal party, will still exercise its beneficent influence and furnish some of the gentlemen of the kindergarten school with what they so much need, a little common sense and ordinary brain power.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the word kindergarten naturally associates itself with infancy and youth, and as I listened here with some patience, and I must admit with some degree of irritation, mjr mind went back to my college days, and I remember committing to memory the reply of William Pitt to Walpole, and the words so aptly suit the present occasion that I may be permitted to repeat them. The reply was:
The atrocious crime of being a young man, which the hon. gentleman has with such spirit and decency charged upon me, I shall neither attempt to palliate nor deny, but content myself with wishing that I may

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
be one of those whose follies may cease with their youth, and not of that number who are ignorant in spite of experience.
Whether youth can be imputed to any man as a reproach, I will not assume the province of determining: But surelly age may become justly contemptible, if the Oippontunities which it brings have passed away without improvement, and vice appears to prevail when the passions have subsided. The wretch that, after having seen the consequences of a thousand errors, continues still to blunder, and whose age has only added obstinacy to stupidity, is surely the object of either abhorrence or contempt, and deserves not that his grey head should secure him from insults.
Much more is he to be abhorred, who, as he has advanced in age, has receded from virtue, and becomes more wicked with less temptation; who prostitutes himself for money which he cannot enjoy, and spends the remains of his life in the ruin of bis country.
The late Joseph Howe, the great Nova Scotian statesman and orator in his fight against the old, entrenched, aristocratic family compact of his day had to put up with taunts similar to those which we have been subjected to and in replying to an hon. gentleman this is what he said on one occasion: The hon. gentleman appears to have leaned over the Castalian spring.
The spring in fable that served a double purpose for the shepherds; they could mirror their fa'ces in the water and also drink the water. Howe continued:
And the hon. gentleman appears to have leaned over the Castalian spring not to slake his thirst or arrange his robe to set off the harmonies of nature, but to fall in love with his own image and die with admiration of himself.
The hon. member for Frontenac-Adding-ton is a Tory in the true sense of the word. He believes absolutely in the principle of protection, political and otherwise. Hon. gentlemen remember the other evening when he was hurling his insults across the floor of the House at us, one of our members asked you, Mr. Speaker, to intercede and prevent him from continuing in that strain. What was his reply? It was: "I want you, Sir, to protect me." Protect him for what? To protect him, to close our mouths, so that in a protected field he might hurl across the floor of this House at us the putrid broth of his distorted imagination.
Now let us proceed with the matters under discussion.

In the first place you remember that in the debate that featured the early portion of the session, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who is the chief financial critic of the opposition, in addressing this House, made this dramatic pronouncement:
I submit that no member of this House should look beyond the question in the resolution; but if we are tempted to go beyond it, if we are tempted to consider ulterior results, then let me say this in the presence of my leader and with his authority, that if this motion carries, if this government resigns, and if he is called upon to form a govenment in this House, he will undertake the task. He will undertake to carry on that government from session to session without dissolution.
That was the statement made by the hon. member for South Wellington at the time he was asking the support of our good Progressive friends to turn the government out of office. But what did he do a month afterwards? We find the same hon. gentleman making this pronouncement:
I ask the Progressives whether they will join us and send the whole question back to the people for a solution at a general election.
And when I heard the hon. gentleman make that statement I said to myself, " Consistency thou art a jewel." The amendment which is now before the House is another of these inconsistencies. We all remember that on January 18, of this year, in speaking on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne and in discussing the question of a tariff advisory board the right hon. leader of the opposition made the following remarks:
Whatever may be said for a tariff commission, there is need-

-of no tariff commission to inform this House, or to inform any fair-minded man or woman, that agriculture to-day, in respect of the tariff, labours under a disability, and a disability which it is the duty of this House at once to remove.
If that principle is true with regard to the disability which my hon. friend pictured in his mind that agriculture suffered under, why is it not true with regard to the automobile industry? In this House a whole afternoon and an evening were spent in discussing the question of the reduction in duty on automobiles, and the figures quoted are sufficient to prove to any reasonably-minded man that this House, according to the dictum of my hon. friend in regard to the' duties on agriculture, should

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
at once have taken the step and reduced the duties on automobiles instead of waiting for a tariff commission.
The figures quoted by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) v/hen the resolution with regard to reducing the duties on automobiles was before the House, showed with respect to the profits made by one manufacturing concern in this country that an enormous toll was paid by our people to one protected industry. On an original investment of $62,500, without any addition of capital, this company in twenty years paid to its stockholders in dividends $12,851,238. But this is not all. The statement which they have given to the public shows that they have invested in their husiness $31,275,530 and not one cent of additional capital except what the company earned was put in. Therefore, instead of the profits being $12,851,238, the total profit made amounts to $44,126,768 on an original investment of $62,500. I am not one who would criticise any industry on any profit it can legitimately make; but when an organization of this kind in supplying a commodity so largely used as the cheaper priced car is protected by a protective tariff of 35 per cent and is thus enabled to bleed users and purchasers of these cars to such an extent as to make the profits which this company made, I rise in protest against that tariff being continued.
Supposing there was no duty on automobiles coming into Canada, what would be the cost to us? The Ford coupe in Detroit costs $500. If you add $12 for excise tax that makes a total of $512. The Canadian sales and excise tax would then add 10 per cent to the value, or $51.20, bringing the total cost up to $563.20. The Canadian selling price before the reduction in duties was $714.88 according to the booklet distributed by the Ford Motor Company among members of this House. That is, before the duty was reduced we were paying $151.68 extra price on the same car. That amount of $151.68 left in the pockets of every owner of a Ford car in Canada wouid be a nice contribution to the prosperity of this country as it would result in an increased purchasing power amongst a widespread number of people from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Those opposed to the reduction in the duty on automobiles point to the pay-roll and they make the bold statement that if the duty is reduced these companies will go out of business. Will they? The same argument was used twenty rears ago in 1897 when the Fielding tariff was brought in placing 160 articles, including binder twine,

barbed wire and cream separators, on the free list. Have these companies gone out of business? Statistics to-day show that these companies have increased and their business has increased during those twenty years. I think it is a safe statement to make that the cheaper you make a commodity the more extensively it will be purchased. A demonstration of this principle is to be found in the history of the Post Office Department. Hon. members will remember that in 1897 when the then Postmaster General reduced the rate of postage from three cents to two cents there were those in this country who said that our revenues would be crippled. But the result was that previous annual deficits of three-quarters of a million were at once turned into surpluses. Five years afterwards, in 1902, the Post Office Department had the first surplus of more than $5,000 over its operating expenses, and these surpluses went on increasing until, when the Liberal government went out of power in 1911, the annual surplus was upwards of $1,000,000.
The same principle holds true in regard to all the great business enterprises in the world. Henry Ford realized that himself in the great industry which he established1. He was, of course, a pioneer in his line; he believed in the principle that lower prices would increase production, and as production increased, Ford's prices were reduced. The latest statistics we have show that in 1924 we had 653,121 cars in operation in Canada. The proposed reduction on motor cars if applied to that number would mean a vast saving to the people, a saving that would materially increase their purchasing power, and that increased purchasing power would add much to the general prosperity which is now in evidence from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

That brings us down to the question of protection and I am sure my hon. friends across the way will relish the next morsel which I propose to give them. A year or so ago the Canadian Manufacturers' Association circularized the manufacturers of the Maritime provinces with regard to the question of tariff duties and I wish to quote the reply which they received from Mr. Angus McLean of Bathurst, New Brunswick. We notice that

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
our friends the Canadian Manufacturers' Association did not spread this letter very freely throughout the country. He was circularized with others to find out his opinion with regard to this matter of tariff protection and this is a portion of Mr. McLean's letter:
"The principal difficulty we have to face," said Mr. McLean, "is the high cost of protection, brought about by too much tariff protection on Canadian-made goods."
Mr. McLean by the way is one of the largest lumber and pulp men in the Maritime provinces.
We find that almost invariably the Canadian manufacturers charge the Canadian consumer the foreign price plus the protection they enjoy under the tariff. Until the Canadian manufacturer is brought to realize that this is taxing the consumer in the most unfair way and changes his ways we are going to have to struggle and work hard to carry on business in the Maritime provinces. Our chief products are from the farms, forests, mines and seas and we must find a market for those products outside Canada.
What we must have to become prosperous is an opportunity to buy our requirements cheaper than we can under a protective tariff; and, next, we need broader markets for the things we produce.
Commenting on this letter the Manitoba Free Press had this to say:
What the busy and devoted secretary of the Manufacturers thought of this communication can be left to the imagination; doubtless he rent his clothes and put ashes on his head. Mr. McLean is, it may be accepted, regarded as an economic heretic, a lost soul.
What did the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) himself say with regard to this matter of high tariff and protection a few years ago in this House? Turning back to Hansard of 1920 at page 2708 we find that he is reported as having used these words:
We never can have a high tariff in Canada. We cannot have a high tariff in Canada for the most obvious reasons. In the first place, a high tariff is unsound in principle in that it tends to eliminate one of the factors of competition, namely, foreign goods.
And further on:
So I say we cannot have any immediate or high tariff for the reason, first, that it tends to exclude that healthy element of fair conditions, namely, foreign competition; secondly, we have in Canada a territory of wide extent. We have one portion of Canada, newer than the other portion, a more predominatingly agricultural country, newer to manufactures and industrial development, and consequently the advantages of the tariff do not accrue to them as 3ret as they ultimately will accrue to them. They come more immediately to one portion of this country than to* another. On account of these two reasons we must always have in this country nothing more than a moderate tariff under any conditions whatsoever.
In view of that pronouncement of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) six years ago in this House, on what ground does he advocate to-day a tariff wall in this country
brick for brick with that of the United States, the most highly protected country in the world? A few days ago the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) made the statement that the industries of Canada were going down, and he instanced some in his own province which had gone out of business entirely. He left the inference that the people engaged in the textile industry in the Maritime provinces had emigrated to the United States and that the United States so far as textiles were concerned was in a flourishing condition. Now I have here an article which appeared in a western newspaper a few weeks ago and which analyses the textile industry in the United States so convincingly that I cannot do better than place a portion of it on Hansard. It is headed "Textiles under High Tariff." Within quotation marks there appears the following slogan:
What are we striving for? More bread and butter, more bread and butter.
The editorial then goes on:
This is the chant of the striking textile workers in New Jersey. All day long the refrain comes from the throats of pickets. Imagine such a condition of affairs in one of the highest protected industries in the United States! How could there be a strike? Do not our Conservative friends tell us that a high tariff wall insures plenty of employment and big wages? We heard a good deal of that gospel during the federal election campaign last year. Nothing could save the textile business of Canada unless this country imitated our neighbour and increased the duty on the imported article. The fact of the matter is the textile workers in the United States are not on full time and have had tlieir wages reduced because the selling price of the commodities they produce is too high for the consumer to pay. There is no other explanation.
Tariff protection for any business is a sort of legal permission for the manufacturer of articles so protected to add the amount of the import duty to his own catalogue figures and put the additional profit into his own .pocket. The worker may get a little of it for a time. But as soon as the limit of the consuming public's purchasing power 'has been reached the demand drops. So there is no benefit at all to the worker and the slump hits the producer fairly quickly. This has happened across the border. Protection is running true to .form-it is not protecting.
What about Canada's textiles under a low tariff? Take the case of Penman's, Limited, of Montreal and Paris, Ontario, on the strength of the firm's annual statement just issued. This concern operates a string of factories in Ontario and Quebec and the year which has just closed is described as one of the most satisfactory years in its history. It is a well managed and conservatively financied company, and, as a matter of fact, a similar state of affairs in industries which are complaining of conditions, as a contemporary points out, "might be productive of a rather different tone to that from which so much political capital is being made."
In the year reviewed by the statement referred to the Penman company has increased its sales by over a million dollars, increased its operating profits by nearly $50,000, and, after laying aside a substantial

I presume if I quoted from the Mail and Empire or the Telegram or the Orange Sentinel my hon. friend would say Amen. However, to proceed:
By tradition low tariff men, they became, in 1920, protectionists overnight. They were told, and apparently believed, that high tariff duties on agricultural produots would bring them boundless prosperity. Now, after five years of experience, they find agriculture almost on the verge of collapse.
The farmers in the com belt have an enormous surplus of corn and are many of them in real distress. Of what avail to them ds the tariff duity on com? No com ds likely to be imported into the United States in the course of a century because domestic production far exceeds domestic consumption. A considerable portion of the com crop is exported either as corn or meat, and the domestic price seldom rises above the export level.
And what is true of the com grower is true of the cotton planter and the great bulk of fanners in the United States. They are less concerned about the theory of protection than they are about their present condition. High tariff duties were to make them rich, and after five years of experience they find themselves poor.
The big farm organizations are unanimous in saying that whatever benefit may be conferred upon the farmer by high tariff duties on agricultural products is taken away from him threefold by the higher prices which he has to pay for everything he buys, from aluminum to zinc. They blame this, not so much upon the tariff duties themselves, as upon the monopolies which have grown up under protection.
. It is a revival of the Iowa idea which led to a wholesale revolt of the farmers against the Payne-Aldrich tariff law some 15 years ago. This present day revolt of the American farmer against the tariff 4is not to be under-rated. It is not under-rated by men like Senator Capper, of Kansas, a lifelong protectionist, who voted for the Ford ntey - Me Cumber Tariff Act. He warns the manufacturers of New England that the whole protective system may be swept away iby a western tornado unless the east consents .to an immediate downward revision of the tariff.
So much for tariff protection to the farmers of the United States. I hope this information

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
will not be lost upon those in this country who would like to inflict similar disabilities upon our agriculturists.
Now, Mr. Speaker, some time ago I gave certain figures in regard to the loss sustained by the Winnipeg Hydro-electric system in relation to their plant, and I wish to place on record the editorial that I then had reference to, because my remarks were questioned by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Stinson), and I want to put him right. The editorial reference is headed "A theory bowled over by the facts":
Persons who listened during the late election campaign to the argument that a higher tariff would not mean an increase in the cost of living in Canada will be interested in what took place at the meeting of the Winnipeg city council held last Monday night. If they came out of the federal election campaign with an idea that the Argument advanced by Mr. Meighen and his friends was well founded they might put the theory up against the facts as they came out in an actual business transaction. The Swedish company which tendered on two generators for the city of Winnipeg's hydro plant offered to supply them at a price that was $15,000 lower than the tender of a Canadian firm. Sweden, of course, is a long way from Canada. Before it can get its generators into Canada the Swedish firm will have to pay duty to the Canadian government at the rate of 27 per cent, or a total in thiis case of about $30,000. The Swedish firm will also have to pay transportation on the ocean from Sweden to Canada and on a Canadian railway from the port of entry to Winnipeg. The firm is to do all these and yet is able to effect a saving of $15,000 to the people of Winnipeg.
Was there any doubt in this case about the benefit cf outside competition? By buying .this particular machinery outside of Canada at the price quoted the people of Winnipeg are saved $15,000, the Canadian government gets $30,000 duty to help in tax reduction and the railways get the benefit of the long haul from the port to Winnipeg. Faced with these facts, one of the aldermen, a supporter of Mr. Meighen, too, said that he could not vote to keep the contract in Canada under the circumstances. To bar foreign competition, he said, would be to leave the city in the hands of the Canadian manufacturer.
A' tariff that would bar foreign competition would cost every Canadian citizen more money to live just as in this case the barring of foreign competition would have cost the city of Winnipeg an extra $15,000. If the council had gone back on the principle which the majority stood for on Monday night it would mean that every time the city went into the market for machinery it would pay the highest instead of the lowest price. Over a course of years this would run into thousands of dollars which would come out of the pockets of the consumer and the taxpayer. Most of these will agree that they are already paying about all they can stand.
On that occasion the hon. member for Victoria immediately contradicted me. He said that this machinery was not manufactured in Sweden at all, 'but in Canada. I was not in a position to dispute his statement, although I was aware of the integrity and reliability of the newspaper from which I quoted. My hon. friend spoke last Friday in this debate, and no
doubt in the interval he had ascertained the facts, and I think he should have had the decency to put those facts on record in his latest speech. After his contradiction I endeavoured to get in touch with the parties concerned, and knowing that the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) was a former member of the Winnipeg council I asked him to write and ascertain the facts for me. I have before me this letter in reply written by the chief engineer of the city of Winnipeg hydro-electric system:
Replying to your telegram of the 19th instant, the list given below shows the tenders received for 2-6500 K. V.A. generators for the Pointe du Bois Plant:
Swedish General Electric Ltd	$143,700,000
Canadian General Electric Co., Ltd	 159,200,000
Canadian Westinghouse Co., . Ltd	 161,000,000
C. A'. Parsons Co., Newcastle-on-Tyne.. .. 159,200,000
The contract was awarded to the Swedish General Electric, Limited, on November 30th, 1925, and the machines will be manufactured in Stockholm, Sweden.
If there is any other information you would care to have in connection with this contract we would be pleased to let you have it at once.
Not content with that, I wrote to the agency of the Swedish General Electric Co. in Toronto, and the letter which I received from them, dated February 19, confirms the information given to the hon. member for North Winnipeg. Now I put these figures on record and repeat the statement which my hon. friend from Victoria contradicted, and 1 ask him to make whatever apology he deems fit in public decency for calling in question the facts when I first submitted them to the House.
Before dealing with the budget, Mr. Speaker, let us consider briefly the legislation which has been before the House for some time. It has been said by some members that this is sectional legislation. Let us examine some of it. Old age pensions-is there any one in this House who will say that that is a sectional matter? Every province will benefit by this legislation provided it takes advantage of it. I know cases in my own constituency of men who were pioneers, who cleared the land and raised large families, and who now in the twilight of life, through no fault of their own, find themselves almost the subjects of charity. Is there any reasonable, sane citizen to-day who in this country of prosperity, individual and collective, would deny to these unfortunate people the right to have their declining years made as happy as possible? Revaluation of soldier settlers' land-surely that cannot be termed a sectional matter. It is applicable to every soldier settler from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Settlement of crown lands-that possibly is somewhat sectional, for the Dominion crown lands are largely in west-

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
em Canada. Those are fertile lands and simply require to be cleared. Cut in the western country the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have seen fit to invest, I should judge, in the neighbourhood of one thousand to fifteen hundred dollars on certain quarter-sections of their land to convert them into what they call " ready-made farms." They build a small house and a small stable and fence the quarter-section. These improvements make the "ready-made farm" attractive to the settler. AVell, if it is good business for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do that, is it not equally good business for the Dominion of Canada to spend a similar amount of money in making our crown lands more attractive to settlers?
The next matter I wish to discuss is the Hudson Bay railway, with regard to which we have had some very conflicting statements. I have in my hand some of the statements made by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) at his nomination convention in the city of AVinnipeg last fall. He said that increased immigration and the completion of the Hudson Bay railway were two of the needs of western Canada which the Conservative party would remedy. The right hon. leader of the opposition, speaking in Regina, said that Canada is too vigorous, too virile and too proud to see the Hudson Bay railway carried to within seventy or eighty miles of completion, and then left, a spectacle to the world. We were told, during the campaign in Yorkton, that the Conservative party should be credited with the construction of the Hudson Bay railway; my opponent said the railway was started by a Conservative government, and made the boast that it would also be completed by a Conservative government. Bearing that in mind, Mr. Speaker, it was rather disquieting to read in the newspapers during the recent by-election in West Middlesex a statement made by the hon. member for 4 p.m. South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland).
He is a good stalwart Conservative, and in regard to the Hudson Bay railway is reported to have said:
That >is the whole substance of this by-election and it is up to the electors of West Middlesex to decide on this change of platform which has as its main plank the expenditure of some $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 on a Hudson Bay railway, which can be of absolutely no use to us and which may not be a particle of use to the people of the west. We must not be selfish, but, until Ave are satisfied that this project and its great expenditure is feasible, it should not be started at this time of heavy tax burdens. If you vote for J C. Elliott you are committing yourselves to the spending of nearly $3,000,000 for over ten years for Mr. King's special little railwav 
On the platform with the hon. member for South Oxford was the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins), a colleague of the hon. member for South Winnipeg, but the newspaper account makes no mention of any protest by the hon. member for Marquette.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I refuse to have my hon. friend interrupt me for the purpose of making a speech; I do not mind answering a question. However, that is not all. We have the Ottawa Journal, a Conservative newspaper, making some statements in regard to the Hudson Bay railway which are rather at variance with those made by the hon. member for South Winnipeg and by his leader, which I would like to make a matter of public record. My first quotation is from an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Journal under date of March 17, 1926:
The first monetary instalment upon the Progressives' price for keeping the King ministry in office was paid in parliament on Monday. It was in the form of $3,000 000 in the estimates for the Hudson Bay railway. It is $3,000,000 thrown at icebergs, seals and wolves.
Some hon. MiEMBERS:	Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext:
I think I had better read the rest of the editorial.
Canada is still burdened with railway deficits. Our Transcontinental, built specifically to haul grain, gets

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
comparatively no grain (to haul. Our ports of Quebec, Halifax, and St. John, into which we have put millions, are largely unused. Most of tbe wheat of Alberta, and some of the wheat of Saskatchewan, now goes through the port of Vancouver. In addition we are putting more millions into the harbour of Prince Rupert; rebuilding the harbour of Quebec; propose spending $55,000,000 more on the Welland canal; and talk about [DOT]deepening the St. Lawrence waterway.
Nine million people, with a debt of $2,300,000,000, plus staggering provincial debts, plus war-peak taxation, are faced with these realities. Yet here we have a government, just returned from a smashing at the polls, brazenly proposing to extract $3,000,000 from the taxpayers for an insane railway project, so that it may mock the public will and purchase retention of office.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South Winnipeg and the hon. member for Marquette stand as dumb as oysters and permit this Conservative organ of eastern Canada to make that statement unchallenged.
At a time when debt reduction is vital, when decrease of taxation is our more challenging need, we are being plunged further into a morass which has already swallowed twenty millions and which, on a conservative estimate, will swallow thirty millions more.
The "patient oxen" of the Scripture had nothing on the people of Canada. Yet there is a limit. And the limit has been reached, we think, when a government begins using the public's money to scoff at the public's verdict.
Again I ask if the hon. member for Marquette and the hon. member for Winnipeg will endorse that editorial. I have another editorial from the same paper under date of February 12, 1926:
Of all the asinine reasons advanced for complotion of the Hudson Bay railway-and their number is legion -the lowest in intelligence is that it was begun by the Conservatives. As a matter of plain record, it was begun by the Liberals. In 1910 the Laurier government started it by building the swing bridge to The Pas, over the Saskatchewan river, and in 1911, just prior to the general election of that year, let to J. D. McArthur the contract for the first section of the Hudson Bay railway, 185 miles. It was largely to pay for this work that the Conservatives were called upon to vote over $3,000,000 in 1914.
But what does it matter now who started it? Is it to be seriously argued that just because Liberals and Conservatives sanctioned something years ago that has since been demonstrated as folly that the folly must be persisted in ?
The people of Canada are not now much concerned with the Hudson Bay railway's origin. They are concerned to see that thirty millions of good money is not thrown after twenty millions of bad money; and their concern will not be appeased by tu quoque arguments about the parties responsible for the evil.
Again I ask those hon. members if they assent to those statements which appeared in this Conservative paper. The Hudson Bay railway is by no means a sectional proposition. It is a necessity, and time will demonstrate that it will work to the benefit of Canada as a whole. I have here an article reporting certain statements made by Senator Robertson in the city of Toronto some little
time ago, which sets out fairly the facts in regard to the future of that road. The article is as follows:
The senator said it hat completion of the line would make it 'possible to tap the iron ore deposits of Belcher island and would proviide a route whereby that iron can be taken to the coal fields of Alberta. Belcher Islands are on the east side of Hudson bay, north of James bay. Their iron mines, says, the story in the Toronto Star, "furnish ore that is said to be higher in quality than the mines that furnish the ore for Bessemer steel. It has a 62 per cent content of hematite as compared with about 50 in the American mines. It can be economically handled in Alberta, where there is coal, gas and oil (in large quantities, making the sort of industrial proposition which made Great Britain an industrial nation. The climate of Alberta is also milder and conditions are ideal for industrial development."
In the course of the interview, Senator Robertson provided an answer to the question: "Is another outlet needed?" He is quoted as saying that when the big tracts of northern farm land are opened up there will be more grain than existing routes can handle. Then "the Hudson Bay route will be imperative." The senator predicts also the development of a water route between Port Nelson and Moose Factory, at the south end of James bay, "which will connect the heart of the west with Ontario and Quebec with cargoes moving both east and west."
One could go on and enumerate the advantages of the completion of the Hudson Bay railway to the people of the whole of Canada, but the matter will no doubt be threshed out more fully when the resolution dealing with the Hudson Bay project is before the House.
The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), in addition to criticizing the Hudson Bay railway, had some things to say in the House a few days ago with reference to western Canada. Here is what he said on that occasion:
This 'budget as a .whole is what might be 'termed a Saskatchewan budget. That statement deserves "a little explanation. The general policies in Saskatchewan seem to be policies of annihilation and assassination rather than protection-
What did the hon. member mean when he made that statement. What are the policies in Saskatchewan that are policies of annihilation and assassination?

We have in Saskatchewan a province that is second to none in Canada from	an agricultural point	of view, and	inevery other way. Let me give my hon. friend a few statistics. I will quote from the Monetary Times, and I do not suppose the hon.	gentleman will offer any	objection	tomy authority. That paper says:	That thegross	debt per capita in	the	province	ofSaskatchewan is $66 and the net debt $33. The gross debt per capita for Ontario is $87, and the net debt is $30. In	the	province	of

Saskatchewan we spend per capita $4 on education. Only one province in Canada spends an amount higher than that, and that is the province of British Columbia. The per capita expenditure of British Columbia for that purpose is $6.64; in Saskatchewan it is $4, and in Ontario $3.38. We have an educational system in Saskatchewan that is equal to any in Canada. No other province in the Dominion, no state in the American union, has on its statue 'books more advanced legislation for the general benefit of the great mass of the people than has the province of Saskatchewan. How, then, does my hc.n. friend get away with the statement that the policies of Saskatchewan are those of annihilation and assassination?

The hon. member for
Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hoeken) in a speech last week advocated the imposition by the government of an import tax on American publications coming into this country. For what purpose? There are good American magazines. Personally, I have taken the National Geographic Magazine for the last ten years and find it a splendid magazine. Why does my hon. friend want these magazines prohibited from coming into Canada?-because that will be the effect if the duty is increased. If my hon. friend and his associates would advise the Canadian people to get good material for reading instead of spreading throughout the country 
reckless Tory propaganda that is so obnoxious to a large proportion of thie Canadian reading public, it would not be necessary for them to come to this parliament and ask for an increase in the duty on American publications. Here is an example of the kind of sentiment the hon. gentleman is trying to spread throughout the country. This is how it reads:
Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King was elected in Prince Albert, Sask., with a majority of over five thousand. That did not startle the country. Anything less than five thousand majority would have been surprising. Mr. King has the honour, if it be such, of representing a constituency sit retching up to the Arctic circle, and with a voters' list that reads like a directory published in some city of the Ukraine. One poll which The Sentinel had an opportunity to examine contained 178 names, only two of which were English, and about seventy-five per cent of them ended with "sky." It is rumoured that the Eskimos voted solidly for the Prime Minister, and the "sky's" were ninety-nine per cent in his favour. There was great rejoicing about it in Ottawa on the night that his success was announced. But in the quiet midnight hour, when W.L.M.K. finds it hard to get to sleep, it must be somewhat depressing for him to think that he had to go to the last north and find a constituency on the northerly boundary of the northern province of Saskatchewan in order to get a seat in the House of Commons, whence he can give leadership to the sixty-one French-Canadians who form two-thirds of his party in the House.
And yet the editor of the newspaper that published that libel on the people of Saskatchewan and on the people of Canada comes here and asks the government to place an import duty on American literature and keep it out, in order that he may spread such kind of propaganda as this through his advertising columns. I should like to make a fitting reply to such action, but	in	the	mood in	which
I find myself I am afraid I might say something for which I might afterwards be sorry.

speechtext:
Instead of doing that I
will give the well-considered opinion of a newspaper editor of high standing in this country, the editor	of	the	Saskatoon	Star.
Here is his reply to this editorial, and to other articles of a similar nature, which have appeared in the Toronto press:
Saskatchewan has many citizens who were born in foreign countries and is proud of the industry they have shown in their private	affairs and of the	publicspirit they have shown	in	their	relations with the
people of native or British stock. In Saskatchewan

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
no distinctions are	made, so harmoniously do	thevarious dements an	the	province's	population	livetogether. Here all	are	Canadians,	citizens of	the
Dominion.
Elsewhere in this country no such broadminded and tolerant notions prevail. Since the Prince Albert byelection which sent	Mr.	Mackenzie	King back to
parliament, certain newspapers published an central Canada have repeatedly sneered at the character of Saskatchewan's population and insulted the intelligence of Saskatchewan electors. One writer referred to the "middle-European aspect of the voters' list" in Prince Albert riding. Another said the significance of the by-election was that Mr. King had to go to the least British of all the constituencies to find a seat. These, however, are mild statements, comparatively speaking. One Conservative journal published in Ontario was kind enough to say that the vote of a bull moose or jack rabbit would be as intelligent politically as the votes cast by some Prince Albert electors.
It may appear superfluous to answer this sort of thing with statistics, but a few numerical facts may be illuminating if they reach the notice of the scoffers at Saskatchewan. Census bulletins published since 1921 deal with such matters as school attendance and literacy in that year. Here are some census findings: The percentage of children between seven and fourteen attending school was 88.85 in Saskatchewan, 91.87 in Ontario. Of the whole population over ten years old 93.47 per cent in Saskatchewan and 96.55 per cent in Ontario could speak English. Of the whole population over five years old 87.85 per cent in Saskatchewan and 92.99 per cent in Ontario could read and write.
There is a small difference in Ontario's favour in each instance, but Ontario has centuries of history to Saskatchewan's decades, Ontario is more densely .populated, it contains fewer remote and new settlements. The insults to Saskatchewan occasioned by recent political events are not justified by the facts of the situation. But they are more than mere errors of statement. They show a contemptibly mean and narrow concept of Canadian! sm.
And I wish, Mr. Speaker, that some of our editorial writers in the editorial sanctums of Toronto would take this article to heart. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) in the course of his address the other day, made the statement that nobody would invest a dollar in Canada under the present government. He said:
The two things we require in Canada in order that we can make out of this country what it is designed to be is, first, people and, second, capital, but this whole plan is devised to make it impossible for any man who has money to put it into Canadian industry because he is penalized the moment he does so whether he is a Canadian or not.
Before replying to that statement permit me to read another statement which he made. He said:
Why, one industrial city the size of Hamilton consumes more beef cattle in a single year than the whole Dominion exported last year, and that was the greatest exporting year we have ever had.
Let us reason out the last statement before we undertake to analyze the first. That is the statement that the city of Hamilton or a city of that size consumed more beef cattle in a single year than was exported from Canada during last year. What are the figures? For the year ending March 31, 1926, we exported beef cattle, one year old and upwards to the number of 228,107. By packing house experience and by butchers' methods, I am told by the statistical branch that the average weight per head of these is 450 pounds dressed beef. Then 228,107 cattle at 450 pounds each dressed beef would make the amount of 102,648,150 pounds of beef. The population of Hamilton was 114,151 at the last census. That would mean, if my hon. friend's statement was correct, that each man, woman and child in the city of Hamilton used per year 900 pounds of beef. There are 365 days in the year, and I suppose in Hamilton, as in other places, they are not all meat eating days either. Therefore each man, woman and child in that city would consume per day on an average two and a half pounds of beef Just imagine, if you can stretch your imagina tion to that extent, in the city of Hamilton the aged man and woman in the twilight of their days, the middle-aged man and woman, the sun-kissed maiden and the stalwart youth, the babe on its mother's knee, all vieing with one another, munching beef in this meritorious task of extending the home market in Canada. That leads me to the conclusion that the author of this statement of the beef eating proclivities of the citizens of Hamilton will go down in the public records of this country as the greatest beefer in the political life of the Dominion.

Bearing that statement in mind, let us examine the other statement by the hon. member, that nobody would invest a dollar in industries in Canada under this government. What are the newspaper reports for the last two months in that regard? Let me put a few of them on record in answer to my hon. friend. The first I put on record is of April 15, 1926, from Fredericton, N.B.
April 14.-The agreement under which the International Paper Company will develop Grand Falls, on the St. John river, was completed here late this afternoon, and now bears the signatures of the presidents of the International Paper Co., and the Fraser Companies, A. R. Graustein and Archibald Fraser, respectively.
Under the provisions of the agreement a block of 20.000 horsepower-13,000 primary power and 7,000 secondary power-is reserved for the Fraser companies,

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
who will embark in the newsprint business with the construction of a 200 ton daily capacity mill on the Restigouohe river, at or near Campbellton.
The International Paper Company will also take out a paper manufacturing charter in New Brunswick. These and other industrial developments now scheduled for immediate undertaking in New Brunswick involve expenditures running, it is estimated, to from twenty-five to forty million dollars.
Another quotation, from Sudbury, Ontario, March 29-and if I mistake not Sudbury is not far from where my hon. friend from East Algoma comes. It reads as follows:
Sudbury, Out., March 29.-An important announcement respecting the future development of the nickel industry in Sudbury district was made at the Rotary luncheon to-day by J. L. It would, however, necessitate a considerable home-building programme and add several thousands to the town's population.
Let me read a few more. This is from Hamilton under date of February 9:
Indication of improved industrial conditions in Hamilton was given to-day by the National Steel Car Co., here, in announcing that the plant was working upon the largest single order ever received. The company is building for the T. and N.O. railway three steel coaches and six steel baggage cars. Both orders are for delivery early in the summer.
This is dated New York, February 8:
The ou*right sale of the ten million dollar bond issue recently floated here for the Manitoba Power Company, by Kissel, Kinnicutt and Company, was reported today.
Proceeds of the sale are to be used by the Canadian concern for the erection of new projections in the western province.

Confirmation of the coming establishment of a new artificial silk industry at Drummondville was given today by two organizers of the Canadian Celanaese Limited, Dr. Rene Clavel, of Basle, Switzerland, and Charles L. The building and plant equipment will cost $7,000,000, it is said.

Announcement is made that a 60-ton per day sulphide plant is to be added to the Thunder Bay Paper Co., here, supplementary to the 400-ton paper mill announced, would be built in consequence of timber limits having been obtained from the Ontario govern-

ment. Work is to be started on the sulphide plant as soon as ground conditions are suitable this spring. Construction will give employment this summer to between 300 and 400 men.

The sale of 4,200 square miles timber limits at the legislative buildings on Saturday brought an additional revenue of $500,000 to the province.
The next one is dated Montreal, March 28:

The last one I will cite is dated Toronto, April 28:
Announcement was made here to-day that the Spruce Falls Power and Paper Company, Limited, had been granted a provincial charter for operations af and near Kapuskasing, Ont., involving an investment of $25,000,000.
And so on all along the line. These are only a few of the statements appearing in the public press showing that this country is going ahead industrially and agriculturally and that all along the line we have prosperity and progress. The beacon lights of general prosperity are burning from the Atlantic to the Pacific, while in this House of Commons of Canada we find some of our Conservative friends fiddling and the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nidholson) engaged in the Herculean task of trying to drive down the throats of the unsuspecting citizens of Hamilton the whole exportable surplus of Canadian beef.
Just a word or two with reference to the budget and its provisions. Is there anything in the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) anything that would injure any portion of Canada? The reduction in the duty on automobiles, the reduction in the postal rate, the reduction in the income tax-all these are for the benefit of the whole population of Canada. Our hon. friends from the Maritime provinces have this further advantage under the budget, namely, that the preference extended to Great Britain can be taken advantage of only if the trade comes through Canadian ports so that this will benefit more materially the Maritime provinces. Can hon. gentlemen from the Maritime provinces, who realize in their hearts that the budget proposals are in their best interests, vote for the amendment which is after all the shadow while the budget is the substance?
What do the people of Canada think about the budget? Let me read a few brief editorial

The Budget-Mr. Barber
references from east t-o west. This is from the Vancouver Province:
Among post-war budgets, the one presented yesterday is notable for several reasons. It shows a country swinging upward on a wave of prosperity. It shows increasing trade and buoyant revenues. It indicates an honest and successful effort to meet and clear off a portion of our accumulated obligations, and it gives evidence on the part of the government, of a desire to meet the wishes of the Canadian people for reduced taxation. . . . Altogther, the budget is one which does credit to the government and the Minister of Finance, and should prove highly popular in the country.
This is from the Calgary Herald:
The Herald repeats that the government has taken a step in the right direction. The immediate effects of lower taxes will be appreciated. The new policy will probably not affect the national revenue, as more money will be released for productive activity. That has been the experience of both the United Kingdom and the United States.
This is from the Winnipeg Tribune and I am sure the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) will appreciate anything that appears in the Winnipeg Tribune:
The budget produced by Mr. Robb yesterday is excellent in some respects. It provides the taxpayers of the Dominion with much needed relief, and in direct form so that the relief can be appreciated.
The article goes on to enumerate the reductions and then it says:
All these are reductions of which the country will most heartily approve. The budget is obviously a bid for popularity and in a degree a successful one.
This is what the Edmonton Journal says:
Mr. Robb's budget was full of agreeable surprises. He was expected to reduce the income tax, but on nothing like so extensive a scale as he has done, while in addition we are to have two cent postage again, beginning with July 1, the receipt tax is abolished, the automobile duties come down, and relief is given to the taxpayer in numerous minor respects. . . . Under the circumstances, the ministry is to be especially commended for doing the right thing. The benefit accruing to the country will be far-reaching. ... As for the general effect of the lowering of taxation, in developing a better spirit throughout the country, in encouraging fresh enterprize and in making the Dominion more attractive as a field for settlement and investment, it is bound to be very great.
Just one more quotation. This is from the Vancouver Sun:
With the first real, Liberal-minded budget since pre* war days, the Mackenzie King government is to-day sitting on top of the world in Canada. Reduction in income tax, two-cent postage, elimination of the receipt tax, further exemptions in the sale tax and the reduction of automobile tariff will create a great wave of public approval throughout the Dominion.
In conclusion let me say as regards some of my hon friends across the way: Around them at the present time the political black robe is about to be wrapped; their funeral requiem is being sung; for some of them the wake is being held, that i3 for those who will vote
against the provisions of the budget, and there will be for them no political resurrection when they go to the country and when the public intelligence of the electors of Canada will carry them and what remains of the old Tory party to the grave of their political incapacity, infidelity and imbecility, unwept, unhonoured and unsung.
Mr. HARRY J. BARBER (Fraser Valley): Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) must feel better. I know if I had that much cn my chest I would certainly feel better after having had an opportunity of relieving myself of it. We have listened patiently to the arguments advanced by our friends opposite in support of the budget as brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) a few weeks ago, and if the government's case is no stronger than the hon. member for Yorkton has presented it, then I am afraid they will fail to convince this House and the people of the country that the present budget is in the general interests of Canada.
Before proceeding to a discussion of the budget itself I want to refer for a moment or two to some remarks made by the hon. member. He told us that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had experienced some trouble in Prince Albert, but he did not mention the fact, as rumoured, that the right hon. gentleman had desired the constituency of Yorkton but had found the price a little too high.
