subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Yorkton brought up the question of bargaining between groups in this House, and I shall refer to the matter later on. For the moment I may observe that the budget now before us has been described variously throughout the country as a Robb budget, an election budget and a Forke budget. As I see it, it seems to me that portions of it may well be termed an election budget, while m other respects it may be described as a Forke production. What have we witnessed in this House since the seventh day of January? We have seen a government which was defeated at the polls bargaining with groups in parliament and even sacrificing the principles of the Liberal party as laid down by its great leaders, in order that hon. gentlemen may retain office. And the present budget I consider another bid on their part for support. The hon. member for Yorkton denied that there was any significance in the talk about bargaining between groups. I have here a clipping from a Toronto paper dated Toronto, March 28, which reads in part:
J. S. Wooclsworth, Labour member of parliament for Winnipeg North Centre, in a speech at a labour gathering here Saturday night, stoutly denied that Labour's representatives in the federal parliament had entered into any agreement with the Liberal government.
Mr. Woodsworth said the fact that the Conservatives and Liberals at Ottawa were evenly balanced had helped labour tremendously in getting what it wanted. If, he sand, there were 12 Labour members at Ottawa, instead of two, the Labour men would be in a position to get almost any legislation they wanted.
Claims Credit for Pensions
Mr. Woodsworth considered the old age pensions bill was a Labour victory.
I do not intend to deal with the question of old age pensions, and as a matter of fact I had little opportunity to discuss the bill when it was before the House. But I may tell the hon. member for Yorkton that he is no more anxious to see the aged of Canada cared for than we are on this side, although I fear that a host of them will have passed to the great beyond before there is any relief from this piece of legislation now before parliament.
The budget, I say, is another bid for support. The reduction in income taxation and the favourable trade balance are heralded by the government as evidence of prosperity in Canada at the present time, but I think the Prime Minister would find it difficult, if he made a tour -of Canada, to convince twenty-five per cent of the people that they are enjoy ing prosperity at this moment. We have had ample testimony to the contrary from farmer

members who have been deploring conditions during the session. Indeed, all the evidence goes to show that tihe farmers as a class are not prosperous. Furthermore, thousands of labourers are leaving the country, and that is no indication of prosperity among the workingmen. The firm of Penman's has been referred to; it is about the only textile industry which has been mentioned in this House. But if any hon. member will go through some of the smaller towns in the province of Ontario he will find numerous mills which have gone behind over $40,000 during the past year. So that there is no great, prosperity in that direction either.
That part of the budget providing for a reduction in income tax cannot, in my opinion, be called a Forke budget if what I read in the press is anywhere near correct. I have here a clipping which reads:
When -the Canadian Council of Agriculture met the Cabinet the other day the members, expressed themselves strongly against the reduction dn the income tax.
Last year according ito recent figures there were exactly 3,061 farmers in Canada paying income taxes, and the sum total they paid was $162,000. This chicken feed was contributed by 530 Ontario agriculturists, to the amount of $19,351. In Quebec 42 paid $3,775, which was just about half the sum 'that British Columbia farmers paid. In the Canadian west farmers appear to have a reasonable view in respect to their responsibilities. In Saskatchewan 1,492 farmers paid $70,956. In Alberta 663 farmers paid $49,894, though Manitoba fell down with only 171 farmers paying $6,303, but this was nearly twice what Quebec paid	
In 1925, 168,000 persons employed in non-agricultural occupations contributed to the income tax collected $13,973,000.
In 1924 Ontario and Quebec paid $44,000,000 out of the total of $56,000,000 paid in income and war taxes.
And this brings up another question. If the government proceeds to rip the vitals out of industry who is to pay the taxes? Where is the government to find that six or seven hundred million dollars necessary to meet the yearly liabilities? Land taxes look to be in sight.
The budget, in so far as it affords relief in connection with the income tax and postage, has been well received throughout the country. The reduction in income taxation is welcome even though it is rather late in coming; the fact is that the people have been anxiously looking forward for four long years to some relief in this respect. If the people have been obliged to practise economy in order to make ends meet and to discharge their obligations to the state, they are perfectly reasonable in expecting that the government of the country shall also economize. Has there been any attempt on the part of the government to retrench? The government last year spent-more than they did the year before, and according to the announcement made by the Minister of Finance, with the legislation before the House and the supplementary esti-

The Budget-Mr. Barber
mates, the expenditure will be still greater this year. In the last four years millions of dollars have been expended on unnecessary public works, abortive royal commissions, worthless immigration schemes, and if present reports are correct, millions of dollars have been lost through the lax administration of the Customs department. All these unnecessary expenditures have been incurred in spite of the statement in the Speech from Throne:
Every effort will 'be made to reduce expenditures.
We are certainly not disposed to bestow much credit on the government for the taxation relief announced in the budget. Without doubt the most important factor in our financial success of the last fiscal year has been the bountiful grain crop. I think the hon. member was right when he said that Canada had been blessed with a kind Providence during the past year. This enormous crop, in addition to the very large exportations of raw materials, has no doubt accounted for the surplus.
What have other countries been doing while Canada has been standing still? Let me quote the remarks of President Coolidge in presenting the 1925-26 budget to congress:
The establishment of a system of drastic economy in public expenditure which enabled us to pay off about one-fifth of the national debt since 1919 and almost cut in two 1 he national tax burdens since 1921 has been one of the main causes in re-establishing prospertiy.
The Australian commonwealth in four years reduced its income tax by forty-seven per cent, calculated on a per capita basis. New Zealand for the year commencing April 1923 reduced its income tax by 20 per cent, except on incomes derived from debentures; in 1924 this reduction was increased to 33| per cent. Its net debt was reduced in the three years from 1921 to 1924 by about $55000.000. Then we have Great Britain struggling under her enormous war debt. Let me quote from the budget as brought down by the Chancellor of the Exchequer a few days ago:
Mr. Winston Churchill was able to fcelil that British trade was improving, that the nation was richer than last year, that the exchange rate was being maintained, that return to the gold standard had made for stability, that the bank rate was no higher than before the war, and that prices were not increasing. More than that, England, during the past six years, had reduced her floating debt by over $3,000,000,000.
I also note that the excise profits tax put on in 1915, with an assessment ranging from 50 to 80 per cent, was terminated in 1921. During all this time no great effort has been made by this government to reduce our na-14011-1921
tional debt or our taxation. On the contrary, after increasing the sales tax from three to six per cent, they merely reduced it to five per oent. They imposed a new tax on receipts, and increased the cheque stamp duty.
No doubt the return to penny postage will be popular with all classes, but I regret that do provision is made for a corresponding reduction in the rates of postage on drop letters and postcards. I have always understood that the Post Office was never intended to be a revenue producing department. Therefore I hope the reduction in the postal rates will not interfere with the continued efficiency and further extension of rural delivery, and that the department will not be forced to continue its policy of employing underpaid rural mail carriers.
The Minister of Finance points to a large and favourable trade balance, but he does not. add that large numbers of our people have not been able to share in the wealth produced by our expanding trade. Naturally, our raw materials figure largely in these exports, for instance, agricultural products, the products of our forests, pulpwood and pulp, and the products of our mines; these make up the bulk of our exportations. I will not attempt to analyse all the figures relating to our export trade, but will confine myself to our exports to one country. I do so because this branch was referred to particularly by the Minister of Public Works in the course of his speech last week. I mean our trade with Japan. It is very noticeable, Mr. Speaker, that whenever oriental matters are mentioned at Ottawa, immediately oriental propaganda is set in motion at the coast. I have before me a clipping from a Liberal paper in the city of Vancouver, of a report which appeared in its issue about two weeks after a certain resolution was placed on the order paper. It is all the more remarkable that the statistics quoted by the Japanese consul are similar to those used by the Minister of Public Works the other day. I am sorry he is not in his seat, for I should like to know from him why he did not quote the figures for 1925. No doubt he confined himself to those for the preceding year because 1924 was one of the biggest years of business we have ever had with Japan. In 1924 our exports to Japan were $26,991,860; whereas for 1925 they had dropped down to $22,046,486. 1 have received from, the department of Statistics a copy of the figures sent to the Japanese consul in Vancouver, and they are
The Budget-Mr. Barber

for 1925. The Vancouver paper to which I have referred headed its report in this way: Japan spends $25,163,278 in Dominion-Vast Trade Growth Between Two Countries Shown-Consul's Statement-Country	Favours Canadian Products,
Figures Reveal.
I have analysed the figures sent to the Japanese consul in Vancouver, and the larger items appearing as exports comprise the following :
Wheat	 | 6,735,859
Cattle hides	 192,089
Cedar and other logs, shingle bolts.. ..	1,545,422
Wood ipu:lp		2,421,824
Aluminum in bars	 1,517,814
Lead in pigs	 2,504,952
Zinc spelter	 1,988,139
Raw asbestos	 321,322
Total	$17,227,421
So we have this substantial proportion representing raw materials out of a total of $22,050,721, As to wheat, I see by a report from Japan that the Japanese are now raising about 25,000,000 bushels per year, and every* effort is being made to increase the production. An application was made to the governing board this year by the agriculturists of Japan to impose a higher duty on foreign wheat, and it was explained that the day was not far distant when they would be in a position to raise sufficient grain to supply their own requirements. Included in that list of exports is an amount of $104,137 for flour. That is all the flour manufactured from our wheat which was exported. We find the list of imports largely made up of foods and supplies for the Japanese who reside in the province of British Columbia including ale and beer $9,810; spirituous liquors $52,661; fruits $167,615, as well as items such as dried fruits, beans, corn, peas, rice, and vegetables in cans. We also imported from this cheap labour country $65,244 worth of incandescent lamps, an import which I believe materially affects one of the industries in this province. I have given this simply as a sample of what the balance of trade really means. We are exporting our raw material in order to make up this so-called favourable trade balance.
One of the main points of the budget is the reduction of the tariff on automobiles, to which the last speaker devoted a considerable time. I believe the term I mentioned earlier in my remarks might well apply to this subject-the Forke budget. The credit for this resolution goes not only to hon. gentlemen to my left, but also to hon. members from the province of Saskatchewan. We admit that Saskatchewan should receive some special consideration at the hands of this I Mr. Barber.]
government; having produced not only the
largest crop of grain but also the largest crop of cabinet ministers of any province in this Dominion. They have no doubt promised their constituents that they will bring back the bacon, in the shape of cheaper automobiles; their speeches fairly bristle with automobile statistics. We are of the opinion that the Prime Minister allowed himself to be swayed by the third party which has everything to gain and nothing to lose in these tariff reductions. I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that this is only the beginning; it has already been intimated that other cuts will follow, and we may expect the boot and shoe industry, the cotton goods industry, the furniture industry and others to receive similar treatment to that accorded the automobile industry.
I stated that the government was forced into line by the Progressive party. They were apparently forced by some 5 p.m. party, because we find that during the last election campaign the Prime Minister stated on numerous occasions that there would be no further reduction in the tariff until a tariff commission had investigated those industries likely to be affected by such reductions. When this House met we were presented with a Speech from the Throne, in which the government expressed themselves very clearly, as follows:
-thait changes in the tariff should be made only arter the fullest examination of their bearing upon both primary and manufacturing industries and that representations requesting increase or decrease of duties should be made the subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the necessary qualifications to advise the ministry with respect thereto. A Tariff Advisory Board will accordingly be appointed forthwith. This board will be expected to make a careful study of the customs tariff, the revenue to be derived therefrom and the effect of the tariff and allied factors on industry and agriculture.
The Prime Minister kept his word and appointed a tariff commission, whose duty it would have been to advise the government on this very matter. Then came the budget, with its drastic cut in the import duties on motor cars and accessories, affecting one of our greatest industries. Did this tariff board inquire into the matter before action was taken? No; this was one time the Prime Minister broke his word and did not keep his promise to the people of this country. He failed to have the board investigate this industry. That should have been done, and if it weTe found that the automobile industry was making too great a profit, a reasonable cut in the tariff could have followed.

The Budget-Mr. Barber
The Minister of Finance, in introducing this portion of the budget, said:
There is a pronounced sentiment throughout Canada that the automobile industry enjoys more protection than is .needed to maintain it on a reasonably profitable basis, and in deference to that sentiment we propose a downward readjustment of automobile, motor truck and motor cycle duties.
The minister seems to have acted altogether on sentiment, and I believe he is mistaken in the sentiment of the people of Canada. He may know what the people of the praire provinces think, but the pronounced sentiment of the people throughout Canada is not that the automobile industry enjoyed too much protection. In my own province, where I believe we pay more for Canadian cars than in any other province of Canada, owing to the long freight haul, the feeling is that Canadian cars are altogether too high in price as compared to those across the line. The feeling in my province is that the government should have investigated this industry long ago; its books should have been thrown open to a body of experts and the report of that body acted upon. The people of my district, and of many other districts as well, have suffered under the tariff policy of this government, but they are loyal to the core; loyal to Canada and to Canadian industry. For the sake of a few dollars on a car they do not want to see one of our greatest industries closed, thousands of workers driven to the United States, and cars imported into British Columbia from Seattle.
Many of the speakers opposite and to my left have been very unfair in their arguments in support of this budget. I would like to refer to one statement made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). He quoted the price of the McLaughlin Buick sedan as given in an American magazine, which price I believe to be correct. If the hon. gentleman will make inquiry he will find that the advertised prices of all American cars cover the bare car at the factory. To that price must be added taxes, freight and equipment. The price of this same car manufactured in Canada was also given correctly, but why was not the hon. member fair enough to state that the Canadian price included taxes and equipment? Included in that price were the following items: extra tire $25.20; tube $4.65; chains $12; bumper $15; sales and excise taxes $135.75; freight $40; tank of gas and handling charge $10, making a total of $242.60. It must also be remembered that 40 per cent of the parts of this same car had to be imported from the United States, under a duty averaging 30 per cent. It is also admitted that the trimmings and finish of the Canadian car are
very much superior to those of the American car.
It has been charged that these big firms, in their protests against this cut, have been bluffing, but I think we find as a rule that big business firms do not resort to very much bluff. The General Motors Corporation has been singled out. This is a big concern, and I find that the Canadian factory is one of twenty-eight branches. I am advised that so far as profits are concerned this branch has always ranked twenty-eighth, with the exception of one month when it ranked twenty-seventh. I have made inquiries concerning the export business and I find that this end of the industry is handled for the twenty-eight factories of General Motors through a New York organization, and that in spite of the British preference this branch lost over $200,000 on their export business last year. This is accounted for by the immense mass production of the United States, and is the reason why you can buy a McLaughlin car quite often in London for less than you can in this country. In spite of the preference, which is in our favour, the immense production in the United States enables them to sell cars more cheaply in the Old Country than can be done through this Canadian factory. I do not think there is any bluff in the matter as far as these people are concerned, because I have noticed already that a trainload of Buicks has arrived in Winnipeg from their Flint factory. There has been considerable argument advanced as to what the position of the Ford Company will be. They are not worrying, for the simple reason that the American Ford car will not be placed in the Canadian market. This is provided for by an agreement entered into at the timie of the establishment of the Canadian factory when the parent company agreed not to enter the Canadian field.
Mass production accounts for the lower priced car in the United States. Here is one fact which is responsible for it: Very expensive machinery is required to stamp out several parts. On account of the cost of this machinery a certain addition to the cost of each oar is made. At the Flint factory $1 is charged for the use of this machinery, Whereas in Canada the charge is $60 for each car. The executives of many of these automobile concerns have unanimously reported that they cannot carry on if these tariff reductions continue in effect. From what I have mentioned already, I do not think that we can consider their representations as bluff.
The Budget-Mr. Barber

Furthermore, we must take into consideration the appeals from the labour people. I have here a copy of The Labour Leader, which calls itself Canada's National Labour Weekly, and it contains an appeal addressed to the members of the House of Commons. The appeal reads as follows
An Appeal to the Member of House of Coan/mons of Cauada
Representing, as you do, the citizens of this great Dominion, "The Labour Leader,'' on behalf of the men who work (in the Canadian automobile factories and the various factories that make /parts and accessories, numbering about 25,000, with about 100,000 women and children dependent on tfiem, earnestly request you ito refer the clause in the budget that deals with the tariff on motor cars to the new tariff commission, so that these workers may have an opportunity of placing their views before them. Gentlemen, forget your political parties, and lend a hand to these hard-working toilers.
Then we have a statement from Controller Joe Gibbons, Business Agent of the Toronto Street Railway Employees' Union. He says:
"I believe that the Dominion government should appoint a tariff commission of, say, five men-one to be a representative of Labour, and one a manufacturer. This commission to (have the power to examine the books of Canadian motor car manufacturers, and as a result of their finding, to determine the tariff on imported cars and parts and to name a fair selling price for the respective Canadian-made cars."
Then we have a statement from Mr. Lew Lewis, president of the Toronto Typographical Union, in which he says:
"While the reduction in the price of small cars looked good to the worker, I believe it only fair to the workers in automobile plants that the whole question should be held for twelve months and given to the tariff commission, so that the workers of Ontario could appear before them and state their views. It is an awful thing to, with one stroke of the pen, jeopardize the jobs of 25,000 men overnight!"
The following press comment is also of interest in this connection:
The Reid Press, a largo printing house in the city of Hamilton, on Monday last placed their employees on half time owing to the cancellation of some $70,000 worth of printing orders that they had on hand from the General Motors of Canada and another Toronto automobile plant. This shows the far-reaching effect of the recent tariff revision, and is another good argument to show that more careful study should be given this subject before a change is made.
What do the American people think of these tariff reductions? I have here a special wire to a Canadian newspaper from New York which says:
The proposal of greatest interest to this country, however, is the reduction of the 35 per cent duty on automobiles to 20 per cent on cars valued at $1,200 or less and to 27^ per cent on cars of greater value. To American manufacturers who have no factories in Canada the prospect for increased sales there will be welcome, but in a larger sense it ia gratifying to note Canada's willingness to lower her 
tariff barriers against American products at a time when our own tariff policy embodies the quimtessimo of selfishness.
Now this is a very important industry boasting a total production last year of $110835,380, an increased production over the previous year of $22,000,000, an industry which paid $17,249,270 to employees during the year 1925. I should now like to quote again from what the hon. member for Sherbrooke said on Friday night. The hon. member gave the following quotation as an indication of industrial prosperity.
There were manufactured in Canada during 192S, 124,000 cars, worth $82,000,000. . . . Export shipments from Canada were the highest on record, the total value of automobiles and parts exported during the year being $39,000,000.
This is pointed out as one of the indications of prosperity in Canada, and still the intention is-according to the budget, and according to the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite-to wipe this industry out. I cannot consider the representations made to the government and to parliament a bluff. I consider there is something to the appeal made on behalf of the automobile industry, enough at any rate to satisfy us that the case should be investigated before taking such drastic action. I have a suggestion to offer in this connection; I should like to carry the bacon home just as well as the members for Saskatchewan. The suggestion I should like to make is this: that the government amend this resolution by leaving the tariff as it was, and immediately have a thorough investigation into the whole industry commenced by the tariff commission. Let the government strike out the sales tax and the excise tax. By eliminating these two taxes, equal to ten per cent, you will have almost if not as great a reduction in the price of cars as you will have under this tariff reduction, and the industry will have a chance to survive. I have not been able to compare the new prices with the old prices of automobiles, but I have noticed the price reduction in Fords, which runs from $15 to $40. This is certainly not equal to the ten per cent reduction which would be given by the elimination of the two taxes referred to.
Now, I wish to refer to the question of immigration, one of the big problems of Canada. In this country we have a railway system, an industrial skeleton, and vast areas of vacant land, sufficient for a population twice the size we have at present. We need more people; there is no doubt about that: this government during the last four years spent millions of dollars on scheme after scheme of immigration. They spent over $3,000,000 in one year to bring in 110,000

The Budget

Mr. Barber
people. What has been the result? The emigration was greater than the immigration. The policy of the government might be termed a minus instead of a plus one. It is a negative quantity; it is one of loss, not one of gain in population. Under this policy we have been unable to hold our own people. Ever since this government came into power in 1921 there has been a steady drift of population from this country to the United States Over half a million people have had to leave their own country. They had no chance here; they loved Canada; they were the very best of our population, industrious, self-reliant, progressive, bent on making their own way in the world and providing for those dependent upon them. The half million the United States gained from Canada in the last few years are worth more to that country than four times as many people drawn from central Europe. I do not hold out any more hope for success under the present scheme of the government than has been achieved under the policy of the government for the past four years.
I wish to refer to the opinion given in the British House of Commons, by Lady Astor on April 26, as follows:
In the House of Commons to-day Lady Astor appeared as an advocate of British settlements in the United States instead of Canada. Colonel Amerv said the government had no official confirmation of the statement that the new American quota system would increase the British admissions to the States from 34,000 to 85,000. He added it was British policy to encourage migration to empire countries, but most of the emigrants to the States were indusitnailasts, for whom there was little or no demand in Canada.
Lady Astor, "Are we not most fortunate in getting our industralists into America," (cries of "Oh") "so long as there is no work for them an Canada?" 6he asked.
Kinflock Cooke, M.P.; "We don't want them to go to America."
That is the present situation and the opinion in regard to these new schemes.
There is another immigration in regard to which I should like to see the tables turned. I refer to the oriental immigration on the Pacific coast. A resolution on this subject was placed on the order paper of the House some time ago, but owing to the curtailing of private members' day it was withdrawn so that an opportunity might be given those from British Columbia to discuss this question along with the general immigration policy of Canada. For the information of those who were not in the House in 1922 when this question was thoroughly discussed and very ably placed before hon. members by the various representatives from British Columbia, I just wish to say that oriental immigration dates back to 1886. The first Chinese eame into British Columbia in that year,
and 90,328 had entered up to the end of 1924. Japanese immigration commenced in 1905, and up to the end of 1924 the immigration amounted to 21,706. Furthermore, 5,381 East Indians entered Canada during the same period so that up to the end of 1924 the Asiatic immigration amounted to 117,415. Consider the source of this supply-800,000,000 facing us on the Pacific slopes of this country. There are 60,000.000 in Japan, 340,000,000 in India, 400,000,000 in China. It is estimated that we have in British Columbia 50,000 to 60,000 orientals, or one in ten of our population. We cannot afford to absorb many more from such a source as this. The improved transportation facilities make this problem all the more serious. We cannot afford any longer to leave our door ajar. This is not all. What about the increase? First remember that there are twenty Chinamen to every Chinese woman, and only two Japs to every Japanese woman. The number of Japanese will soon outstrip the Chinese. The increase is hard to discover, because the white people have to register the birth of every child, while it is difficult to get a record of all the births of orientals. Oriental children do not come into the world like our own children do. We have nursing homes, doctors and nurses, but not so with the oriental: A baby is born in the gloom of Chinatown or in the solitude of a Japanese home and scarcely anyone knows anything about the event. During the ten year period from 1910 to 1920 the estimated Chinese increase was 172 per cent, and the Japanese, 218 per cent. Our best guide is the growth of the school population. I have here a report from the Minister of Education for British Columbia which reads:
The minister stated that whereas there were 1,422 young Jaips attending public schools in 1923 and 1725 in 1924 there are no less than 2,414 enrolled in 1925. The Chinese attendance, on the other hand is going down slightly. It was 1.346 in 1923 and 1,423 in 1924, but this year it is 1,313. Of Hindu children there are 26 as compared with 30 last year and 16 in 1923.
The white school population, which would naturally be expected to be increasing at a greater ratio, is relatively standing still. It was 92,120 in 1923 , 93,156 in 1924 and is this year 94,228. In other words, the number of white children attending the public schools of British Columbia in 1925 has increased by two and one-third per cent over 1923, while the attendance of Japanese children has increased by seventy per cent.
I present the figures of one man who has made a great study of this problem, and as to the matter of increase he states:
With 60,000 orientals at present in our province, estimating at the present rate of increase, in thirty years from now we would have 34,882,643 orientals in British Columbia. This is not taking into account the fact that we have oriental young people growing up and that many of them will marry.
The Budget-Mr. Barber

I cannot agree with this gentleman that these 35,000,000 odd orientals will remain in British Columbia. They will drift east and enter into competition in all lines of business, with the result that white labour will gradually be squeezed out in your great industrial centres. That peaceful invasion of the east has been taking place during the last few years; orientals are doing business in many of your towns and cities to-day. It is estimated that in the city of Toronto last year two million dollars was paid to Chinese laundries. I was surprised to see in Hansard of 1922, when this subject was before the House, an hon. member stated that in the city of Ottawa at that time there were 65 Chinese laundries, 4 grocery stores, and 21 restaurants, conducted in such a way they could not be recognized as Chinese.
As I have said, the number of orientals in our province number one to every ten of the whites. After a few years of marriage these young orientals will increase with amazing rapidity. In California there are 150,000 Japanese with 40,000 children, and they say that in 1949 at the present rate of increase there will be enough to outvote the white population in California twice over. I am citing all these figures, not to scare hon. members with the "yellow peril", but I want the House to be impressed with the seriousness of the situation from a racial standpoint. The Americans brought the negroes over from Africa and when it was too late they tried to get rid of them, but it cost them a bloody war of four years among their own countrymen while the black man looked on. They could not send them back to Africa after they had made such increases in population, and to-day there are approximately 14,000,000 of them in the United States where they are increasing by leaps and bounds. We do not want a race war. This is more than a British Columbia problem; it is a problem that must be dealt with by Canada. We must deal with the oriental problem before we are inundated, crowded out and displaced by the flood of orientals.
One man has said:	"Why not follow the
example of China and build a wall around our country?" We are not asking that a wall be built; we are not asking to keep out the oriental who wants to vist our country or to do business with us, but we want the gates of immigration closed so that they cannot come here, settle and become citizens of Canada. A race which you cannot assimilate, you cannot associate with geographically. Oriental and occidental cannot successfully mix. If the oriental had been on this continent first, well 	;
and good; but it is a fact that the white man was here before the oriental. White people pioneered the great Pacific province, endured many hardships and made many sacrifices in order to build up our country. The white man developed our rich valleys and laid bare the rich resourecs of our great province. The orientals are not pioneers. They come into our developed valleys, buy land, settle, multiply, spread and cause the original settlers to sell their property at low prices and leave.
This brings me directly to the economic side of this problem. The white man cannot compete with the oriental. The oriental can stay and stick; he is the hardiest of all races in God's world; he has been hardened by
8.000	years of heartache and history. You can see the 8,000 years in their very gait. You have seen them walking in single file along the street and their gait shows that for 8,000 years they have walked the narrow passages. They have been trained to suffer hardship; they can stand extreme heat and work long hours; they have a lower standard of living, and yet the white man is put alongside the oriental and expected to compete with him. Is it any wonder that it was estimated that
18.000	Britishers left British Columbia in 1924 for the United States, while 50,000 orientals remained and partook of the inheritance that rightly belonged to our kith and kin? They have not hesitated to take advantage of the opportunity afforded them in this country. Their activities threaten the very life of the Anglo-Saxon on the Pacific coast.
One is simply astounded when the Japanese complain of their treatment by the white man in view of the treatment they mete out to the white man. Canadians are much more generous to the Japanese than the Japanese are to the Canadians. We have no sacred rights in Japan; in fact no white man has any sacred rights in Japan. Japanese in Canada have every agricultural, mineral, industrial commercial and financial opportunity enjoyed by native-born Canadians, but no reciprocal privileges are extended to Canadians in Japan. We cannot own farm land or forests or mineral resources there. In only a few cities can we own anything and even this privilege tends to be swept away rather than to be fortified or extended. We cannot get justice in Japanese courts; Japanese jurisprudence operates in such a way that white litigants prefer to settle all cases out of court. We are discriminated against by Japanese freight boats. For example, if a white man and a Japanese ship from Yokohama to Vancouver the same quantity of rice of the same quality on the same Japanese boat, the white man will be

The Budget-Mr. Barber
charged twenty per cent more than the Japanese.
It is estimated that at the present time the fishing industry is 75 per cent in the hands of the orientals. The milling industry-that is saw mills-is 75 per cent in their hands. Pulp-wood, barrel staves, shingle bolts and cord-wood production is almost entirely in their hands. They control and operate about 35 per cent of the logging industry. In one case in my riding a mill had been supplying the Japanese with cedar in clear cut timbers from selected logs at about $80 per thousand. They no longer purchase these timbers; they export the logs for which they pay about $18 per thousand, ship them on their own boats to Japan, manufacture them by cheap labour and export to the countries of the world. A large quantity of our best cedar is in this way being permitted to be exported to Japan anr in 1925, for instance, $1,325,713 worth of choice cedar logs was taken out of our province by Japanese boats to Japan.
Truck gardening is almost entirely in the hands of the orientals. They are entering in a large way into all lines of mercantile business. They compete against our white people in the grocery, tailoring, barbering, restaurant hotel, taxi and other pursuits. They are eating the heart out of our industrial and commercial life, and more especially our heritage, namely, our basic raw materials such as fishing, lumbering, logging, farming and mining. In the agricultural industry a census was taken and the returns are accurate, being supplied by the Farmers' Institute of British Columbia. It shows that in 1920, 500 Japanese owned some 8,000 acres. 116 Chinese owned some 5.600 acres, 103 Japanese leased nearly 1,800 acres and 368 Chinese leased over 11,000 acres.
A report of the British Columbia berry growers shows that in 1920 there were 234 oriental growers occupying 97(H acres and in 1924 this had increased to 366 oriental growers with 1,4651 acres. They have penetrated our best agricultural districts. In my own riding there is one of the finest districts in Canada where the chief industry is small fruits and mixed farming; it is an ideal spot for the Canadian or Britisher to make his home; but as you pass along those roads you would imagine you were traversing one of the highways of the Orient. I am told that there are about eighty Japanese on one rural mail route in this district. As you drive along the road you will pass groups of little blackheaded children wending their way home from school. Every one of these families is taking the place of a good Canadian or British family and every oriental holding an industrial job
to-day has chased a white man out of the country and across the line. If you replace these with white men we will retain in this country the $15,000,000 that is being remitted every year to the Orient and we shall have people who will contribute to building up healthy communities in this Canada of ours.
What is the remedy? Four years ago this question was before the House with the request that the government grant us exclusion from British Columbia of Japanese immigrants. The government at that time told us that they would give us "effective restriction" which we were assured would give us the same results as exclusion. How has this worked out? Since that year we find a steady increase in Japanese immigration. In 1923, 369 came in; in 1924 , 448 and in 1925, 501. Of these 501, 182 were males, 269 females and 50 children. These are the details according to the report of the Department of Immigration and Colonization for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1925.

What we ask for is some provision similar to that enacted in the amendment to the Chinese Immigration Act of 1923 as respects Chinese. Under the provisions of that act the admission to Canada of persons of Chinese origin upon the payment of the head tax was abolished and the entry of such persons restricted to the following classes:
(a)	Members of the diplomatic corps, or other government representatives, their suites and their servants, and consuls and consular agents;
(b)	Children born in Canada of parents of Chinese race or descent who have left Canada for educational or other purposes on substantiating their identity to the satisfaction of the controller at the port or place where they seek to enter on their return;
(c)	(1) Merchants as defined by such regulations as the minister may prescribe;
2) Students coming to Canada for the purpose of attendance at any Canadian university or college authorized by statute or chapter to confer degrees.
During the fiscal year 1924-25 no Chinese immigrants were admitted to Canada: we ask for precisely the same regulation in regard to Japanese. To show what the Americans have done, the following extract from the report on immigration will be of interest: The new United States immigration quota law was passed by congress May the 15th 1924, after going to

President Coolidge had requested this postponement of the date so that a suitable treaty might be negotiated with Japan. Congress refused; the President signed the bill May 26th, 1924.
This question is one that affects British Columbia particularly at the present time, but it is one in respect of which we feel that we have a perfect right to appeal to the federal government for action. We do not want to create any racial hatred or any invidious discrimination against any people in Canada, but we do want both parliament and the country as a whole to have an intelligent grasp of the oriental problem as it exists today. We should be delighted to follow the example of our friends to the south. They appointed a commission to inquire fully into the whole question, with the result that an exclusion regulation has been introduced there. We would urge the government to appoint a commission to study the problem here, to have all the facts placed before them, and to report their findings. If this is done we have no doubt the proper remedy will be applied. I can assure the government that such a commission would have the heartiest support of the people of British Columbia. We would welcome orientals to such an inquiry. The government and the House might hesitate at the cost of a commission, but I wish them to bear in mind that the federal government has collected in head tax and registration from Chinese immigration the sum of $22,523,921. There is therefore some consideration coming to British Columbia in this matter.
I wish now to refer to a matter which has been mentioned on several occasions and which interests my riding particularly. As I have already stated, there is without doubt a certain amount of satisfaction over the budget, but I know of one class that is greatly disappointed. I refer to mixed farmers, dairymen, poultrymen and fruit men. The government failed to recognize the necessity for protecting this class of producers. They have failed to give the necessary tariff protection, their interests not having been consulted in the negotiating of treaties with other countries. Appeals have been made to the government on behalf of these industries by almost every representative from the districts affected, and there has been pointed out quite clearly the disastrous effect that must ensue from the policy outlined in the budget so far as this par-

tieular section of the community is concerned. This is an important industry and one that should undoubtedly have received the very best consideration at the hands of the government. A large amount of capital is invested in these forms of production. The following table will give an idea of the importance of the dairy business:
Invested in Dairy Business:

The total imports of dairy products for the calendar year 1925 amounted to $2,409,233. In the same period we imported 2,721,606 dozen eggs at a value of $957,780, of which quantity 2,577,400 dozen came from the United States. Butter comes in from the United States under a tariff of four cents per pound, while the United States tariff against us has recently been raised from eight cents to twelve cents per pound, /gainst Australia and New Zealand we have only one cent per pound protection. Eggs come in from the United States under a tariff of three cents per dozen, but their tariff against us is eight cents. We import cheese from the United States under a tariff of three cents while their tariff against Canadian producers is five cents. I notice from the report issued by the Statistical branch that we received from the United Kingdom, the United States, New Zealand and Australia for the three months ended March 31 of this year, a total of 6 755,732 pounds of butter at a value of $2,552,000. In the same period we imported eggs from China and the United States to the value of $863,269. This makes a total importation: of these commodities for the three months mentioned of $3,415,269. In view of these facts surely the dairy industry should receive some concessions from the government. But the fact is that the budget now before parliament ignores our producers altogether.
The government apparently has not given any consideration to the fruit growers, whose market is not protected. This matter has been very fully discussed, and while I am not going to enter fully into it I wish to point out to the House that this industry has been discriminated against. For example, the American tariff on apples is 25 cents per bushel of fifty pounds; on dried apples, 2 cents per pound; on berries 1| cents per pound. All the protection we have is 25

The Budget-Mr. Barber
per cent. The government inflicted a hardship on the fruit growers as well as on the dairy industry of Canada in the concessions they made to Australia and New Zealand in the treaty that came into force last fall. Canned fruit, canned vegetables and fresh fruit were admitted free, while perhaps the most serious injury was the placing on the free list of fruit pulp for canning purposes. Our growers always depended on this market for their surplus product.
Speaking of the Australian treaty, I am reminded of the remarks of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) who expressed the following view:
I am safe in saying, I believe, that there is not much butter manufactured in Canada in winter, the vast bulk of our product being made when the cows are in full milk in summer. The milk and cream offered for' sale in Canada in the winter months goes directly to the dining tables of the land as such. The fact is that, our butter is being made in summer when cream is plentiful and being stored by the creameries and the cold storage plants, if anyone suffers through the admission of Australian butter it cannot be the primary producer.
I am very sorry the hon. gentleman is not better informed on winter production. The department of Agriculture has spent a large amount of money and done a lot of work in order to encourage our farmers to carry on winter production. In this connection, allow me to refer to the report of the Finch dairy station, Ontario. Among the objects aimed at in establishing this station, I find:
(c) encourage the production of winter milk.
I find the report contains a table showing the amount of milk received from December to March, inclusive, and following it is this comment:
The production during the winter months of 1922-23 shows an increase of 828 per cent as compared with the winter months of 1912-13.
This paragraph I have no doubt will interest hon. members:
The operation of the Finch Dairy Station on a commercial basis has demonstrated among other things that an increased output means lower manufacturing costs and permits of dual equipment being installed without unduly increasing the overhead charges. The dual equipment enables producers to reap the advantage from turning out either butter or cheese, whichever happens to be the more profitable for the time being. It is possible to operate the large factory continuously throughout the year and fthus encourage winter dairying.
I wish also to direct the attention of the House to the report of the Superintendent of the experimental farm at Agassiz, B.C. The dairymen in the surrounding country are spending large sums of money not only to provide for winter dairying but also to improve their herds. The record of 22 cows
which have completed lactation periods during 1924 is interesting as showing the improvement that has taken place in the dairy herds. The following summary I desire to place on Hansard:

It is impossible to carry on profitably either the dairy industry or the poultry industry for only three months in the year. Every effort is made to keep up winter production. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the only policy which will tend to solve the problems of Canada is the policy of the Conservative party. That policy was fairly and squarely placed before the people by my right hon. leader, and from coast to coast the electors accepted it wherever it was not beclouded by other issues. The Conservative party is not a high tariff party, as has been charged in Liberal propaganda. The Conservative party stands for a protective policy, which, without permitting the exploitation of Canadian consumers, will protect Canadian markets for Canadian producers, be they manufacturers, agriculturists, or wage-earners. It
The Budget-Mr. Barber

stands for a policy that will give goods produced alt home preference at home; that will build up Canada instead of the United States or some other country; that will develop Canadian resources; that will as far as possible have Canadian raw materials manufactured in Canada; that will provide work and wages to keep Canadians at home; that will build up Canadian communities instead of American or other foreign communities; that will provide home markets for Canadian farmers, purchasing power for Canadian artisans, and traffic for Canadian railroads. In a word, it is a policy that will provide a measure of prosperity for all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now in the third week of this debate. I do not know why it should take so long to discuss a question of this kind when, as anyone listening to the debate will have noticed, nine-tenths of the speakers seem almost unanimous in their expressions of opinion. Apparently there is only one question which has so far divided the various parties, that of the reduction in the tariff on automobiles. I do not know whose are the unseen heads which determine how long this discussion shall last, but I believe they would confer a favour upon a great many members of this House if the debate could" be closed this week. We have had cited on many occasions precedents established in the British parliament; I do not know of any British precedent for a debate of this length. In the English House of Commons the debate begins and finishes within a few days, and I think this House would be doing a good thing if it followed that custom.
After listening to the discussion which has gone on for the past few weeks one begins to realize the ramifications of the tariff policy of Canada. We have had to listen to a discussion on our trade relations which took us into practically all the corners of the globe. Canada exports her goods to not only the various European countries but to the Orient and Australia, as well as other parts of the world. As a result we are brought into direct relationship with all these various countries. After all, trade is barter pure and simple; international trade is international barter. When we send goods to Great Britain they are bound to send goods to Canada in return; when we send goods to oriental countries we

must receive goods from the Orient. That is a fundamental economic axiom which most people who have given thought to this question realize and admit. We could not, even if we so desired, become an exporting country alone. If we attempted to do so, refusing the imports of other countries, it would not be very long before Canada ceased to be even an exporting country.
One of the main questions I wish to deal with to-night is one which has not been touched at any great length by previous speakers. For a short time I would like to deal with the question of the tariff as it affects wages. A great deal has been said about the workingman, how he is affected by the tariff and so on, and I would like to speak in that particular phase of the question. I claim that a high tariff does not mean high wages; on the other hand, neither does a low tariff mean low wages, nor does a high tariff mean low wages. I claim that the tariff plays a very small part in the question of wages, and when we begin to look into the question of wages from the purchasing standpoint we realize the truth of that statement. What determines wages? I contend that wages, speaking in a general way, hover around the subsistence level; that is, an employer is going to pay his employees the amount of money they can subsist on, and not much more if he can help it. If there are certain places which have a higher standard of living, that standard has come about through other causes than the tariff. One of the main reasons why some countries have higher wages than others is the organization of the workers themselves; if there had been no organized labour movement I really hate to think what would be the standard of the workers to-day in some countries. The worker, whether in a protected country or a free trade country, has only one thing to sell; that is his labour power, and as a rule he gets the most he can for it in the market where it is sold. Although it has been provided in the Peace treaty in the past few years that labour is not a commodity, it is just as much of a commodity to-day as it was -when that provision was framed. We find countries to-day in which wages are very low. They are very low in the Asiatic countries. They are low in India, China, Egypt, and Japan. In these countries a very low standard of living exists. Now, the British worker and the Canadian w'orker in the textile mills have got to compete with the workers of the textile mills in China, Japan and India where the wages are extremely low. What is the international view-

The Budget-Mr. Heaps
point of labour to-day on that particular question? It is one of trying to raise the standard of living in those countries where a low standard prevails, because it realizes that is the only hope there is for the workers. We have had a recent example of that in India where the textile workers were on strike in the city of Bombay for many weeks, and where British capital and the employers were engaged in trying to beat down the standard of subsistence among the Indian workers, although it is ait present very low. What was the reply of the British workers in that case? They took up subscriptions in Great Britain for the strikers in India because they realized that if the Indian worker was beaten a time might come when there would be an attempt to force a reduction of wages in Great Britain.
We find another very important factor at work to-day in connection with the international relationship of labour. Within the last few weeks a conference was held in London on the invitation of the Prime Minister of Great Britain. This conference was called for the purpose of establishing an eight-hour day in five of the European countries, namely. Great Britain, France, Belgium, Germany and Italy. Even the employer in Great Britain realized the necessity of the movement. On account of the strong labour movement in Great Britain the employer there was compelled to give to the employee the eight-hour day. But having done so he found himself at a disadvantage in competing with the products of longer hours of labour in some of the other European countries. The consequence was that an agreement was arrived at between the representatives of the five European countries named and they recommended back to the various governments for whom they were acting that they should enact an eight-hour day in their respective countries. The trend of events is such that, as I view it, the same policy will have to be pursued in other countries where the conditions so far as labour is concerned are favourable, because the workers in countries where there is now a higher standard of living is not going to see -that standard lowered gradually in other parts of the world; rather they are going to work for a raising of the standard of living where it is at present unduly low. That improvement is not going to be brought about by any tinkering with the tariff.
What were the conditions of the Indian workers? Mr. Tom Johnson, one of the Labour members of the British House of Commons, was sent to India to investigate
conditions in the textile industries and report back. I shall quote now from a report, taken from the Daily Herald, London, England, of February 17 last, in which Mr. Johnson says: Forty 'millions go to bed ait night having eaten only one meal during the day, and twelve millions perish in an influenza epidemic (because their bodies are so emaciated that they cannot resist the attack.
But where is the evidence that when Brownface supplants Paleface in the governorship (as he must soon do), the ryot and the artisan will be freed from the toils of the landlord and the money-lender? When, recently in Bombay, 150,000 cotton operatives struck bravely and without strike pay for 11 weeks against starvation wages, neither Swaraj nor British raj lifted a finger to assist them.
Indeed, when Mr. Bose moved his resolutions in the Bombay Assembly for a public inquiry into the conduct of the cottom mill industry and for a lak and a half of rupees grant for rice to the starving women and children, he was turned down with emphasis by a combination of Indians and English. What help the strikers received was from their own class overseas, and I am specially commissioned by the workers of Bombay to .thank the British trade unions who sprang so readily to .their assistance and made a successful issue possible.
Now, the average wage of the worker in India at the present time is about $1.25 per week, and India is not a free trade country. The policy of protection is in force there, and yet the product of that country has to compete with the product of Dundee, Scotland. At the same time, whilst the wages of the worker in India were so low-so low in fact that they can only be termed a miserable pittance-the jute companies in India in ten years made $300,000,000 of profits, which is equal to eight and one half times the wages paid in the same period.
I turn from India and come to a consideration of the conditions in Japan. Now Japan is one of the the most highly protected countries in the world. Why, the United States has not got a look-in when it comes to protection. I have in my hand a copy of the revised tariff of the Empire of Japan, with classifications dated 1923. The new tariff was put into effect on July 8, 1924, and the duty under it was increased by one hundred per cent.

speechtext: Is not that a lovely country?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext:
What do we find subsequent to that? In the report of our trade commissioner, published in the Commercial Intelligence Journal of May 1, 1926, I find this with respect to the Japanese anti-dumping law. The report says:
In the supplementary budget for the fiscal year 1926-27, the Japanese government has asked the Diet for the approval of an appropriation of 12,825 yen as the initial cost of the establishment of an antidumping investigation commission. This commission
The. Budget-Mr. Heaps

is empowered to deal with all matters concerning the prevention of the dumping o*f foreign goods which act to the detriment o>f domestic industries. Concurrently with the putting into operation of the new tariff on March 29, the anti-dumping law is to be promulgated by an imperial ordinance and become immediately effective.
There is an anti-dumping law now on .the statute books, but it has never been put into operation. It is anticipated that the revised law, details of which are not yet published, will .provide for the prohibition of the importation of those commodities sold in Japan at the low production cost of fair market price in the country of origin, or when the industry producing these goods is receiving a government or state subsidy, or when they are sold below cost as a result of trade competition.
Competition by foreign firms in iron and steel, dyestuffs, sulphate of ammonia, soda ash and pulp will probably be the first subjects of inquiry by the anti-dumping commission.
I wonder if hon. members of this House realize the significance of a statement of that character. Here we have a nation whose workers are among the lowest paid in the whole world. Yet its government passes an anti-dumping law against nations whose employees receive wages five, six and ten times as high as the wages paid in Japan.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And in the name of labour I suppose?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
of the protection which the manufacturing industries have had, the workers have had no protection at all. The point I wish to stress to-night is the fact that protection gives no protection to the workers.
This is rather an interesting article dealing with a tender that was going to be let by the United States Naval Department. This is what it says:
Shall a contract for building the engines and machinery for six American gunboats be let to a British firm in China employing coolie labour?
This question has been put squarely up to Secretary Wilbur of the Navy department, who comes from California, where the Chinese labour question has been an issue for many years, resulting in >the exclusion of Asiatics from entering this country as immigrants.
The last Congress enacted a measure providing for the construction of six gunboats to be used in patroling Chinese waters and fixed a maximum expenditure of $700,000 for each vessel.
The Navy department made plans *to have the hulls for the gunboats built in China, where they are to be put into service, but to build the Deisel engines to propel them in the Brooklyn navy yard. Later the department decided to install reciprocal engines and have them built in China.
Engineers of the Navy department claim that a sav;ng of something over a million dollars would be made by giving the contract to a British firm in China employing cheap coolie labor.
Of course the Navy department will not permit the Chinese to man the gunboats. American citizens will be called upon to do the fighting if there is any to be done.
We find further how the highly protected steel industries of the United States can actually sell their goods in Great Britain at a lower price than they can be manufactured in Great Britain and about $4.50 per ton less than they sell them to the people of the United States, at the same time paying freight rates over to Great Britain. What happened when in the city of Glasgow not long ago this same United States Steel Corporation put in a tender for steel rails? Who was it that protested against the United States Steel Corporation sending their goods over to Great Britain? The Conservatives and some of the Liberal members of the Glasgow city council were anxious to have the goods imported from the United States, but the Labour members of the council rose from their seats and protested against the dumping of goods which were produced under sweatshop conditions and in the end they won out.
I wish to deal with something which has been dealt with by many other speakers, but possibly not from the same angle. I wish to deal with the budget, and to get away for the time being from the question of tariffs. Some hon members have called it a "prosperity" budget; some have called it a "poor man's"

budget; some have called it a "people's" budget; others have called it a "rich man's" budget. I do not know which of these fit, but anyone can have his choice.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A popular budget.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some have even called it a "popular" budget. I wonder what the average workingman has to look forward to in this budget. It is said there is going to be reduced postage on letters, a reduction in the income tax and the receipt tax is to be abolished. I do not know how much benefit the workingman is going to get from the abolition of the receipt tax. It is not often that he has to buy stamps to put on a receipt. If his saving by the reduction of the postal rate from three cents to two cents is taken into consideration, he might save five cents a month or possibly sixty cents a year. This is not much of a poor man's budget. When it passes this House the worker will have to work just as hard as he did before; he will have to fight his employers just as hard as he fought them before; he will still have the same struggle to exist as he had in previous years.
Some 'hon. gentlemen have stated that to increase the tariff will provide more work. I do not think that is sound economics. High tariff does not of necessity mean more work. What the worker wants is not merely work; the worker should not be classified as a kind of horse who has to work whenever he is called upon to do so, be given a certain quantity of fodder for his day's work, and then go back into his stable in the evening. He ought to be given a higher standard of living rather than to be merely a machine and have profits wrung out of him. The workers want a higher standard of living; they want more of the goods they produce, and the only way in which we can have some prosperity in Canada and other parts of the world is by giving the workers a wage by which they can have that higher standard of living.
Let us see what the worker produces and what he gets in return for his labour. In 1917 there were employed in Canada 552,968 persons in industries of all kinds. In 1923 this number decreased to 446,994, the largest percentage of reduction having occurred in the year 1920-21. In 1920 the number of persons employed in industry was 526,571 and in 1921 it took a sudden drop to 391,203. Why did not my hon. friends opposite put up a high tariff in 1921 when they saw work in Canada gradually dwindling? They did not for the very good reason that they knew

The Budget-Mr. Heaps
very well that the tariff at that particular time could not have served to increase the amount of work available in Canada. There were causes altogether apart from anything connected with the tariff, which contributed to that huge drop in the number of workmen in Canada in that period. The principal factor was the deflation that set in, and no government, at any rate no government as governments are constituted at the present time, could possibly have attempted to settle a question of that nature.
What was the volume of goods produced by the workers in that period? In 1917 the total production was worth $2,873,268,183, and that amount of wealth was produced by 552,968 persons. In 1923 the total production amounted to $2,781,165,514. The figures for the years from 1917 to 1923 inclusive are:

It will be observed from the figures I have given that the total value of manufactured products was greatest in 1920, but we must not forget to take into consideration the value of the dollar at all times. In 1920 the purchasing power of the dollar was quite low; it increased considerably in 1923. It will be interesting to compare the years 1917 and 1923 from the standpoint of the value of our dollar. In 1923 the dollar stood at 153 as compared with 178 in 1917, so that the index value was 25.5 less in 1923 than in the former year. This means that the total value of manufactured products which I have given for the year 1923 as $2,781,165,514, if based upon the value of the dollar as it stood in 1917, would be in reality $3,244,693,100. On the other hand, if we take into account the fact that the wholesale index figure of prices was 243.5 in the year 1920, when our production was largest in dollars, the total value of our output in those twelve months; based upon the 1923 cost of production, would be $2,370,243,362. Perhaps I may put it in this way: In the year 1923, with 446,994 persons engaged in industry, as against 552,968 employed in 1917, there was a tremendous increase in production over the previous period. And if we exclude all salaried persons working in offices we find that in 1917 the production per individual was $5,196 as compared with $6,222 in the year 1923. Now what wages did the workmen receive in those periods respectively? In 1917 the average 14011-193
worker engaged in industry-exclusive of salaried officials-received $760; in 1918, $878; in 1919, $938; in 1920, $1,109; in 1921, $1,002; in 1922, $939, and in 1923. $959. These figures will give us a good idea of what the workers actually produce and what they actually receive in return for their labour, and in view of these disclosures I claim again that no tariffs, whether they are high or low, can greatly affect the situation.
A good deal has been said about the reduction in automobile duties. I cannot help contributing a word or two to the discussion of this question, having interviewed some members of the very large delegation that visited Ottawa a week ago. It is quite true that most of these workers who came to Ottawa did so at their own expense. This is true with very few exceptions. I did the best I could to understand their problem and to ascertain their grievance. Some hon. members went so far as to look into their eyes. I did not do that but I went right up amongst them and spoke to them, trying to gat their point of view. But what interested me was the amount of wages they were getting; I wanted to know what they were paid, seeing how upset they wrere over the reduction in the automobile duties. I do not think there is an hon. member in this House who knows more about the trials and tribulations of the average w'orkingman than I do. I have lived amongst them all my life and I understand something of their problems. The first question I put to these men therefore was as to the amount of wages they received. I found that in the Oshawa factory the great majority of the employees were getting an average wage of between $80 and $85 per month. Later on, moving amongst others of these workers. I was informed that some of them earned from 70 to 75 cents an hour: that would be in the more highly skilled and more hazardous occupations. Work is fairly steady with these people, as I ascertained, but apparently they do not know what the tariff means. "What do you know about the tariff?" I asked; and the general answer was, "We don't know anything about the tariff, but we know that we have had a dirty deal." I then wanted to know what was the nature of this "dirty deal". The answeT I got was that, whereas they had been working overtime before the reduction was made, when they came to work on the morning following the budget they found the gates closed against them. "Who closed the gates?" Well, they held the government responsible for it; they considered that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was to blame for the gates having been closed against them. Now, Mr. Speaker, I say that when an employer



The Budget-Mr. Heaps
shuts out his employees in this way he is exercising a function which in my opinion is far beyond his prerogative; and he is doing something equally unjustifiable in influencing people bo action such as they might not otherwise take. I do not personally believe that the reduction in the tariff on automobiles will have any great effect on the industry in Canada, and I say that, advisedly.
I have here a clipping from the Montreal Star, which paper I am sure no one will claim is in any way biased in favour of tariff reductions. It appeared in the issue of the Saturday following the announcement of the budget and is as follows:
In conservative quarters where Canadian industrial developments are watched closely, the opinion was expressed that the proposed reduction in the Canadian automobile tariff, if adopted by Parliament, would not necessarily mean the end of the manufacture and assembling of American automobiles in Canada. The only direct result of such a change, according to the opinion, would be to reduce their profits. Assembled United States cars, it is explained, have been sold to the Canadian public plus the tariff, thus adding to the profits of the Canadian subsidiaries of the United States companies.
Recently, Mr. Speaker, I received a letter, and it is quite possible that other members from Winnipeg and vicinity also received a similar communication. I have not yet obtained the sanction of the firm to give its name, and consequently I must withhold! it for the present, but I may say that the firm employs about one hundred people. It has threatened to close down if it does not get increased protection for the particular commodity which it manufactures, the tariff protection on which has been reduced by the budget. Let me read this very illuminating portion of the letter:
In addition to the reduction in tariff, we wish to point out to you the handicap we would be working under in endeavoring to meet the United States competition-with the protection on pig lead of one cent per pound as follows:
Canadian pig lead, as j'ou no doubt know, is mined and smelted in Trail, B.C. by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, and they base their price- not on their cost-but take advantage of the one cent per pound duty; and simply base their price on the foreign market, plus one cent per pound, less five cents per hundred pounds f.o.b. Montreal.
Mind you, although the lead is manufactured at Trail, the price is figured at what it would cost to ship the commodity from Trail right to Montreal, which is the port of landing for this class of goods from England and other parts of Europe.
The five cents per hundred pounds is deducted from the imported f.o.b. Montreal price, to assure them the Canadian business.
Further, when we purchase our requirements (as we must do) from the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, they charge us the Montreal price, plu3 the

carload rate of freight to Winnipeg- which is fifty five cents per hundred pounds; for example, if the imported f.o b. Montreal price, less five cents per hundred pounds, is eight cents per pound, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company will charge us $8.55 per hundred pounds delivered f.o.b. Winnipeg, although the lead is shipped from Trail, B.C. They will not sell to us at price f.o.b. Trail, B.C. Such price to be the Montreal price, less the carload rate of freight from Trail to Montreal, and then let us pay the freight from Trail to Winnipeg.
Now, if anybody can beat that I s-hould like him to come forward.

I do wish some of my hon. friends opposite, before quoting from such newspapers, would find out something about them.
This man Heavy was at one time a member of the Cigarmakers' Union and represented that union in The Trades and Labour Council. The Cigarmakers' Union withdrew him from the council on account of his disloyalty to the Trades Union movement. Through a friend, who was about as bad as himself, he got into the Stage Clearers' Union, which was affiliated with the Theatrical Stage Employees' Union. He was then an advertising solicitor and had no connection with the theatrical business.
So he was not even a bad actor.
It was one of those shady deals sometimes put over in the labour movement, by a bad gang who eventually come to their end. The London Trades and Labour Council has also a resolution on their books refusing to give him admission to meetings of the council, although he was born in London and was a resident of that place. His only connection with the labour movement is his connection with the Theatrical Stage Employees, and that union has been told that under no circumstances will the District Labour Council accept him as a delegate. The Labour Leader has been several times condemned as the enemy of the workers. It is a paper which is run by two private individuals for the money they can get out of it. They supported the Conservative party at the last election and opposed the Labour candidates everywhere. They made their advertising rates prohibitive to Liberal candidates at the last election because the Conservative party had them controlled body and bones.
