speechtext:
They have none.
The paper is regarded as the friend of the Manufacturers' Association and profits considerably financially because of its support to that association. Heavy is a member of the Conservative party and is regarded by the Tory machine in Toronto as one of its strong supports. He has no influence in the Labour movement, but on the contrary is regarded as one of the worst traitors we ever had in the Labour movement. It is a matter of court record in Toronto that Brigadier-General Gunn and Mr. Roden, ex-president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, appeared before the metal trades employers in Toronto at the time their employees were out on strike to ask them to vote $5,000 to Heavy to assist him in getting out a Labour paper. At that time Heavy was the secretary of the Trades and Labour Council. It was because of this act of treason while in the Labour movement that he was thrown out of
The Budget-Mr. Heaps

the Trades Council and Cigarmakers' Union. John W. Bruce, general organizer of the Plumbers' and Steam-fitters' Union, openly charged him with being on the staff of the Milwaukee Detective Agency, while operating in the Labour movement. Heavy started court action against Bruce but dropped the case after it had gone -through its preliminary stages. This Charge was based upon the fact that while Heavy was in the bar of one of the Toronto hotels some years ago a card dropfped out of his pocket, was picked up (by one of the men who was with him, and afterwards read. It was a card connecting him with .the Milwaukee Detective Agency.
One recent incident will reveal -the -type of the man. His paper has -made a lot of money because of dts attacks upon Communists and the Red element, but at the last convention of The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, Tom Moore, the president, was opposed by a Communist. Heavy voted for the Communist. This can only be explained on the ground of Tom Moore's refusal to be used by Heavy and his paper to -further their financial gains.
You can tell Hugh Guthrie for me, as vice-president of The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and secretary of the Canadian Labour party, that every time he quotes from The Labour Leader or mentions the name of W. J. Heavy in support of -his theories or party he is insulting every decent trades unionist in Canada. Everything I have mentioned in this letter can be supported by documentary evidence.
Sincerely yours,
James Simpson.
I also have further references to this man Heavy which appeared . in the London, Ontario papers, made by some of the officials of the London Trades and Labour Council. These are very much along the line of what I have already quoted.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley dealt with the question of the income tax, and quoted certain figgures to show what the actual reduction was. I am also interested in the income tax question, although perhaps in not exactly the same way as other hon. members who have already spoken. I have given figures which show that the average
worker cannot pay income tax because his wages do not come within the income tax limits. I have here the figures published by the Bureau of Statistics in that connection, and I want to read some of these figures because they show some rather startling facts in connection with the concentration of wealth in Canada. In 1923 there were 1,181 persons who paid income tax, and who might be termed the highly favoured few. I wish I was in that class; I would never complain about the income tax I had to pay. These 1,181 persons paid $12,022,219.

speechtext: I have already transgressed a self-imposed rule, and I do not wish to go much further into some of the matters upon which I have dwelt. But I wish to say this: We find as a result of the facts which I have given that in the production of wealth the portion which the workers, both men and women, receive out of that which they have produced is extremely small. We find, according to our income tax returns, that the wealth of the country is concentrated practically in few hands. Here in the Dominion of Canada we find a quarter of a million people paying income tax. If that is the case, taking five to a family, it will mean that a million and a quarter people, men, women and children, may have benefited by the reduction of the income tax. But what about the other eight millions of people? What are they getting out of the budget? That is the question that has to be answered, and I do not expect either the Liberal party or the Conservative party to give us much more than they are giving us at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you answer your own question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am trying to show my hon. friend, and I hope the points I have made will reach his mind and stick there. I have been showing to-night how little the worker gets for what he produces. I have been Showing that wealth has been concentrating in fewer and fewer hands; and if the hon. gentleman wants to know what I think, I have no hesitation in saying that I think labour is entitled to that which it produces. The person who is performing a useful function in society is entitled to something more than a mere pittance in life, and to receive when he reaches the, age of seventy a pension of $20 a month. This old age pension should not be necessary in any country. But why is it necessary? There is also, as I have said, a discrimination against any industry or trade which is carried on 'by a corporation or company instead of by a private individual, in that the tax on the incorporated company is doubled or otherwise increased. The Canadian investor in shares of a foreign company pays only one tax, but if he invests his money 'in a Canadian company, as I have said, he pays at least a double tax and 'possibly a triple tax. The obvious result is to render it more and still more difficult to obtain funds for investment in Canadian companies carrying on corporate enterprises in this country.
I think the taxes as now imposed are prejudicial to a certain extent to the individual. The wage-earner who saves up out of his income a certain amount for the protection of his wife and children when he is gone, or for the protection of himself against old age or other disabilities, finds that by investing the proceeds of his thrift in a Canadian company, perhaps the company by which he is employed or in which he is an official, he thereby seriously impairs the amount of revenue which he, in case of incapacity, or his wife or children after him. would receive froo^ the fund which he has laid up against such possibilities.
There are many anomalies in this income tax as we have it. For instance the rural resident who owns his house or his farm pays no tax whatever upon his investment nor upon the value or user of his house or farm. speechtext:
Certainly it is the case, but I am suggesting that if the Minister of Finance undertook to remove these anomalies under the guise of reducing the income tax his work has resulted in a still further increase in the anomalies and not in any reduction in <tihe amount exacted from the

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
people in income tax. In my opinion-and I have a perfect right to my opinion although it may differ from hon. gentlemen's-a more unfair, prejudicial and discriminatory readjustment of the provisions of the income tax law could hardly be conceived than this presented for the approbation of parliament toj day.
Apart from the income tax, certain reductions in customs duties have been proposed, as for instance in the case of sugar, which I understand are made to comply with the provisions of the West India treaty. I think we are entitled to know why there should be any general reduction under present conditions in sugar duties. If we are to give a preference to the West India producers certainly we are in a position to raise the general tax so as to preserve the income which comes to this country from sugar. The tariff does not affect the export trade because in the export trade there is an almost entire remission of the duties paid. It seems to me that before this budget is considered in committee we should have some further explanation from the Minister of Finance of the particular provisions relating to the West Indies.
With regard to the further provision in the case of automobiles, that there shall be paid from the treasury by way of drawbacks of duty, refunds to The importers of component parts entering Canada for the manufacture, the construction, or the assembling of automobiles here, I would suggest that the whole system of drawbacks is wrong. It is simply a covert way of removing a fair protection from one of the great basic industries of the country. I consider the production of iron and steel in Canada as much a basic industry as the growing of wheat; it is the industry upon which a great number of our large industrial interests are founded and sustained. And since this government came into office, by its preferences in favour of Great Britain, by its preferences in favour of Belgium and France and other countries, by its repayment of drawbacks in favour of the United States 

by all this discriminatory legislation it has weakened and impaired the great iron and steel industry of the country. That is entirely borne out by the facts which have been brought down in various government returns. For instance, in the year 1920 we had 1,475 plants engaged in iron and steel production, and in the manufacture of the products of iron and steel. In four years, up to 1924, the last figures available, that number has been reduced to 1,003. That industry in 1920 had a capital of $624,000,000, which in 1924 had been reduced to $535,000,000. It paid salaries and
wages to 115,700 workmen and employees in the year 1920 and by 1924 that number had been reduced to 78,000, while the amount paid out to these workmen in the respective years was $158,000,000 and $99,000,000. The industry employed materials to the value of $321,000,000 in 1920. I have not the corresponding figure for 1924, but the selling value of the products, all of Canadian manufacture, produced by Canadian workmen, was $640,000,000 in 1920. reduced in 1924 to $370,000,000. The value added by Canadian workmanship and machinery, exclusive of material, was in 1920, $318,900,000 and in 1924 only $174,000,000. So that in the annual production of wealth in the iron and steel industry there has been a loss of $144,000,000, and this is due to tihe insidious and deceptive yet complete manner in which the legislation and the government policy of this country is undermining and destroying a great industry.

speechtext:
I am prepared to show, if necessary, that this diminution in the productive activities of our own people is made up by the large importations which we are making of the same class of goods. That is the reason why although we were employing 115,760 men in 1920, we are employing in 1924 only 78,000-a very considerable reduction, due to 470 odd plants having been entirely driven out of business by the policy pursued by this government.
Now, I do not wish to enter upon a lengthy discussion of the promises and pledges made to the country by the right hon. leader of the government. The first time that his pronounced views on tariff policy came to my special notice was when he was entering upon his campaign in Nova Scotia in October 1921. There his policy was one of protection to the iron and coal industries of the province. On that pledge of protection to those industries he secured the return of a Liberal member for every constituency of Nova Scotia; the electorate believed him and voted for his can-
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

didates. There he said, according to the reports in the press:
Free trade is not the policy of the Liberal party. If dt were, I would oppose it because I believe it would bring disaster to our industries and remove from the farmers the home market, which is practically the only market they have left.
He continued:
Free trade may be all rig hit tfor the wealthy grain growers of the west whose wheat goes to the foreign markets and who do not have to worry about selling their products at home, but it would mean paralysis in the Maritime provinces.
Because of that pledge of the right 'hon. leader of the government he was supported by nearly all the constituencies east of the Ottawa j-iver; they returned an almost solid phalanx behind him in the last parliament. But our anxiety was aroused when we read his address on May 15, 1924, in discussing the budget before the preceding parliament. There he declared that the policy of the Liberal party was:
No more tariffs based on the principle of protection. That is our policy to-day, the policy of the Liberal party, proceeding stop by step towards the goal of greater freedom in matters of trade, never imposing a duty for protection's sake, but always acting on .the principle or the basis of a tariff ifor revenue, and revenue only.
In 1925 there was such a tremehdous reaction throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion-I refer particularly to British Columbia, Ontario and the eastern provinces -against that pronouncement that he broached an entirely different policy to the country. We have his own statement of the grounds on which he appealed to the governor general for a dissolution in December last. We have his pronouncement made at Richmond Hill, where he said that his policy was that of appointing a tariff advisory board so that no manufacturer need feel afraid of sudden reductions in duty until he had had a full opportunity to have his case investigated by the proposed board. He declared then:
I believe the people should be given an opportunity to .pronounce upon a ipo'l icy as far-reaching a3 that which is involved in this method of dealing with the tariff and other problems of taxation. This is another reason why I feel the time of general election should not be postponed.
You have all read in this House the pronouncement which he made in Oshawa on October 19, when he declared:
There .must be groat care and caution used in adjusting the tariff to safeguard the industries of the Dominion. The only way to 'handle the matter of tariff is that a board of advisers, containing officers of the different departments of government, gather information that will be of service to the government in determining a tariff policy. In our opinion this is the only fair and just way to deal with the question.

We returned to Ottawa last January, convened by His Excellency as members of this House. There was very considerable anxiety on the part of the leader of the government on maeting the House as to whether he would be able to secure the support of a majority of the members, his party representing only 101 votes and the Conservatives representing 116 votes. He again approached His Excellency and through him made an address to this House dealing particularly with tariff issues. He knew, just as well as I and other members of this House know, that there are a number of hon. members representing the same province which I have the honour to represent who in their public and private utterances freely and frankly declare that they are in favour of adequate protection for the industries of this country. While he was angling-if that is the proper term to use-for the support of the Progressives of the west, he was anxious to retain the support of the members on his side of the House representing Quebec constituencies where important industries are employing large numbers of men and need a safeguarding tariff for their protection. Therefore the right hon. leader of the government came to this House and through the address from His Excellency the Governor General made a solemn pledge to the House and to the country that changes in the tariff would only be made after the fullest examination of their bearing upon primary and manufacturing industries. That pledge gave some assurance to those people whose money was invested in industry, and to those who were employed in industry, that their interests would not be suddenly dealt with. But it became necessary, 'because of my hon. friends to my left and the leader of the Progressive party, who possesses the entire political authority of this country with no political responsibility except to his own constituents, that a blow should be launched at the automobile or motor power industry of this country. The right hon. Prime Minister had no alternative but to bow the knee to Baal and repudiate every solemn pledge he had given to this country through the mouth of His Excellency the Governor General.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend
admits it. It is recognized by the whole country, and by my hon. friends also. But that is destruction, that is an end to responsible self-government in Canada. It is impossible for the leader of a government to give any pledges to the country or to bind his honour with respect to any proposed programme, because he knows that he is utterly unable to carry it out unless those few gentlemen at my left subsequently endorse it.
We have a clear cut distinction between the tariff and fiscal policies of the right hon. Prime Minister and those of the Conservative party. It is discussed by the members of the House, and clearly recognized, that all measures which have been introduced by the government during the present session and all the changes proposed in the tariff or in taxation are for the purpose of binding to the support of the Liberal leader and the Liberal government those who are not fully convinced of the wisdom of his general policy, and those who are not prepared to give him support on general political grounds. The result has been to undermine public confidence in the government from one end of this country to the other. There are many men who are not so closely interested in the tariff as to care, individually, as to whether a protective policy or a free trade policy is best. But they are suddenly discovering that stability of tariff and stability of commercial and industrial conditions affect tens of thousands of men who thought they were not interested in the tariff, and t-hat they were not effected by it.
It must be admitted that our production is decreasing. I have statistics galore which show that during the last five years we have been ceasing to produce those commodities manufactmed by the industries of Canada; year by year as we produce less we import from abroad those commodities manufactured
The Budget-Mr. Cahan
elsewhere which are taking the place of commodities formerly manufactured in Canada.
If hon. gentlemen will examine the trade returns for last year or for the previous year they will find that of approximately one billion dollars of imports brought into this country, five hundred million dollars represent commodities Which could be produced in 'Canada by Canadian labour, Canadian capital and Canadian machinery. This would and could give employment to at least a quarter of a million people in addition to those already employed, giving sustenance and a livelihood to at least a million more Canadians than we have in this country at present. In other words, if we had what the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) referred to the other evening, a tariff adequate to our needs, we could bring back the half million people who in the last five or six years have gone away, and we could bring into this country and employ at a rate of wages corresponding to that prevailing in the United States and higher than that in England or in continental Europe, workmen and their families numbering five hundred thousand more.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that we never can build up this country; we never can develop it-except for wheat growing-unless we safeguard industry so as to produce in this country those commodities now imported, carrying to the final processes of manufacture the raw materials and other commodities which enter into our factories as raw materials. We must develop all along the line. It is utterly ridiculous to say that you can place this country in a sound and prosperous financial, commercial and industrial condition simply by bringing in farmers from England or somewhere else to grow wheat on the western prairies. Grow wheat? Yes; let us give every possible inducement to the growing of wheat, but let us not forget that if we are to have a general expansion of trade and business; if we are to increase our population to enable us to sustain and pay off our national debt and to reduce the individual burden of taxation, we need a million people, and a million people cannot find places on western farms for at least ten years to come. We now purchase commodities from abroad, thus giving employment to foreign labour. We bring them into this country and pay for them by the raw products of 'Canada which we send abroad, thus exhausting the natural resources of the Dominion for that purpose. If we reverse that policy and manufacture at home we can place this country in a position

The Budget-Air. Cahan
of prosperity unequalled by any other country on the face of the globe. Because we have still in Canada the natural resources, at present unexhausted, which are the very foundations of industry and which will enable us, if we decide to manufacture our own commodities in Canada, to bring them, through the highest processes of manufacture, to a completed state.
Now there is a clear distinction to be noted. I have talked to some of my Progressive friends in this House. I have talked to many of my Liberal friends from the province of Saskatchewan. I am attracted by their complete sincerity in dealing with this trade question, and I think that they realize that many of us on this side of the House are equally sincere. But I wish to say to them that our position is this: The policy of this government, which, to use their terms, is to develop primary industries and to export primary or raw products to foreign countries for the purchase abroad of manufacturing commodities, will show, as it has shown last year, an enormous expansion of export and import trade; but every dollar that we send out for the purchase of commodities abroad which we could produce in this country represents one dollar of value which, if put into circulation in Canada to employ labour and to manufacture commodities here, would be worth five times as much or five dollars, in the domestic trade of this country. Now such a policy-

speechtext:
I am going to expound my theory in a moment, and I think that exposition will fully answer my hon. friend. If he does not think so and will repeat his question at the close of my speech I will endeavour to answer him. I say we ought to give every encouragement and assistance to the production of wheat and other grains of the middle west. Do not misunderstand me with respect to that. I say that at the same time we ought not to neglect and discourage, we ought not to discriminate against and destroy, the industrial life of these eastern provinces and of the province of British Columbia. We of the Conservative party, I think, should be prepared to co-operate in giving essential assistance and supervision to the incoming immigrants in the west who are now being located chiefly on these western farms. We should be willing to assist in every way in increasing the supply of farm labour until that supply is fully met; we should assist in every reasonable measure to consolidate settlement in the western railway belt, to ensure reasonable freight raites for the transportation of surplus products of grain from the west to the

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
seaboard-either east or west-and even assist it in its transportation overseas. But the farmers of this country are not the only body who contribute by their labour to the productive activities of this country, and my contention is, because it is my sincere belief, that the men who produced $465,000,000 in 1923 and $640,000,000 in 1920 of the products of iron and steel are adding just as much, dollar for dollar, to the wealth, the prosperity and the wellbeing of Canada as the workmen of the west who produced $640,000,000 worth of wheat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend
one reason for the conditions in agriculture in the United States, especially in the grain trade.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is doubtless
aware of the Capper Bill.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I sat the other night by a
member of the Senate of the United States, the very able and representative member of one of the western states, and he said, speaking of the relative situation and the condition of the farmers in the western United States as compared with the farmers in our own northwest, that we had conceded to the Canadian farmer reduced freight rates, reduced cost of transportation, which placed him in the most enviable position of any farmers in any country of the world to-day. That was his view; I do not profess personally to know sufficient about it.
I quoted the other day the sworn evidence given before the railway commission as to the cost of carrying wheat. I will not repeat, but I am waiting, as my hon. friend doubtless is. with considerable anxiety the production in this Houses of the actual figures to show whether or not that wheat is bearing the cost of its transportation to Atlantic ports.
I am convinced also that my Progressive friends from Alberta and Saskatchewan must and do recognize that their position is exceptional in this country. Theirs is a branch of farming carried on under special conditions, requiring special encouragement, to be made prosperous by special forms of legislation and co-operation in government administration. So far as I am concerned, and so far as most intelligent people whom I represent in the city of Montreal are concerned, I believe they are prepared in every reasonable and effective way to give what assistance they possibly can. I know that some hon. gentlemen have referred to me as representing St. James street. Now St. James street is not in my constituency.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
K the hon. member will
look at the legislative programme of this government he will find that it is designed for that purpose. Whether or not it will be effective in achieving that purpose I cannot say.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the hon. member tell
us what it is?

speechtext:
In the first place, it is
proposed that we should reduce, to the extent-suggested by those who have made a careful estimate-of $50,000,000, the mortgages outstanding on a certain body of farmers in the west called the soldier settlers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the soldier settler not
also located in the east?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Are they not a federal
responsibility?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

No, I do not understand
so. However, I am getting off my subject. The large appropriation which has been made for soldier settlers was not directly and ostensibly for the purpose of settling them because they were soldiers. I understand the country was taking advantage of the fact that a large number of Canadians were willing to go on the land, and some preference was given to them rather than to foreign settlers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Is the hon.
member objecting to that?

I told the hon. member
I would answer his question when I got to the end of my discourse. I am convinced that, as they enter more and more upon diversified farming in the west-

tell us how to farm.

I am not telling my hon.
friends how to farm; I am not even suggesting it. But all the wisdom of the world is

not concentrated in western constituencies. I have great respect for the hon. member who interrupted me, because I realize that he knows more about farming than I can ever hope to know. But I can state the grounds of the faith and the confidence that is in nle, and I say that when the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) will undertake, in a duly protected market, to raise wool, for instance-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When my hon. friend undertakes to raise these products in a properly safeguarded market he will increase his inr come ten times what it is to-day, and that trade would be far more profitable to him than all the wheat and grain grown on his farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, and I know what it is before the hon. minister asks it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would you put a duty on wool?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, certainly I would put a duty on wool. My hon. friend has asked that question time and again in this House, as if he were questioning some ignorant class of scholars who did not understand the basis of that industry, and trying to make them think they dare not place a duty on wool. I would put a duty on wool and assist every farmer who is raising sheep and lambs. I would produce wool in this country as far as it could be consumed by our factories, and make Canada deal independently of every foreign country as far as possible. I think this country in its wisdom will soon find it is unprofitable to send out its wool in car loads for manufacture in other countries into clothing, to be shipped back in bales and parcels in finished form to keep us warm in winter. The sooner we produce within our own boundaries every commodity which is natural to the country, and manufacture it here in all its processes, the sooner we shall enjoy industrial activity and commercial prosperity such as has not been known in this country during the last twenty-five or thirty years.
For my part I say-and I say it clearly- that I do not believe the industrial prosperity of Canada can be maintained by a government which is not prepared to challenge every hostile tariff which it finds opposed to the admission of its own products. It is abso-
lutely necessary that we Should pursue a policy of tariff stability so that Canadian industry will know exactly where it stands and not be subject to these interminable changes of tariff such as hon. gentlemen opposite have introduced within the last five years, changes whidh have only one result, namely to destroy our manufacturing industries, send people out of the country, and, as I said before, undermine the entire confidence of those who have money to invest in our own undertakings.
Situated as we are in close proximity to the United States, it is absolutely necessary that we should take conditions which prevail there into consideration in dealing with the question of tariffs. I do not wish to discuss at length this automobile question. ( have read every document which I have received through the mail from those who advocate a lowering of the duty and also from those who advocate the retention of the duty I have read the addresses of hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House dealing with the matter. I am accustomed to deal with facts and figures; I am accustomed to deal with statements of account, and I say that I am not yet able to form an opinion as to whether there is any just cause for reducing the tariff on automobiles a single one per cent. I do not believe there is a gentleman on the opposite side of the House who really knows all the facts.
I find that located within the limits of the city of Montreal, a place where I did not imagine any person was interested in the production of automobiles-I thought that was confined to Ontario and to a few towns in Ontario-there are twenty-eight establishments which have put before me their claim that the automobile industry should not be prejudiced or destroyed because a large proportion of the products of these various concerns find their way ultimately into finished automobiles. The matter has equally broad ramifications throughout the entire length and breadth of the country, and I repeat, hon. gentlemen are pledged, before they make such a reduction, to have a thorough public investigation before their tariff commission.
I quite agree that any industry which is protected and safe-guarded by public legislation of any kind, by tariff legislation or otherwise, becomes to that extent quasi-public in its nature and it assumes special obligations to the public as long as it enjoys that safeguarding provision or protection. It continues in many cases to be privately-owned and privately-managed, but it becomes subject to certain limitations arising from the equally fundamental rights of those to whose well-being its products contribute. It exists

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
and it must exist as a profit-making enterprise; otherwise it cannot exist under our modern industrial conditions because unless it yields a profit it will not continue to function in this country. But the public has the essential right to receive from that enterprise or industry the most effective service possible at prices which, providing a stable and certain profit for the investor, will nevertheless stimulate home consumption and tend to improve the general standards of living in this country in which its products find their market. Such an industry should be in a position and should be required by the public and the government to take advantage of all improvements in art and science in order to extend its operations as reasonably required and in order to produce commodities of the best quality at prices commensurate with those which are paid in other countries operating under similar conditions.
All this requires ample funds and credits and that no industry can obtain if it is to be the victim of rapidly changing tariffs and values which are the bane of all manufacturing industries. Therefore this country owes, I think, due protection to its industries, but no industry has the right to use the public protection which it receives through the tariff or otherwise for the purpose of profiteering at the expense of our domestic consumers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did Mr. Ford have to say on that very thing the other day?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hon. members do not like to hear that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will deal with Mr. Ford in a moment, but I want to lay down the general conditions as they appear to me. I am speaking simply for myself and giving my own view. Therefore it has been admitted by successive leaders of successive governments of this country that if the stability of an industry is threatened it has paramount right to a full inquiry before some independent or semi-independent tribunal before final judgment and condemnation is passed upon it. Such full inquiry, such independent investigation has never been accorded to the automobile industry of this country.
The tariff changes which 'have been proposed are admitted by the Minister of Finance to be due to public sentiment and not to a public inquiry into the fundamental conditions surrounding the industry. If public sentiment is to prevail in a country such as this in preference to a judicial or quasi-judicial inquiry, there is no innocent man who would be kept out of the penitentiary. There is no place in Canada for public sentiment which is another word for individual or general prejudice. You must deal fairly with these men whom you have invited to come into this country, and establish factories here.
In ease profiteering is established, I wish to repeat what I stated the other day that in my opinion a reduction in the tariff is not the efficient and advantageous way of dealing with the problem. The removal of the protective principle, whether that principle is embodied in a tariff or other legislation, serves only to destroy the domestic industry and to transfer to foreign competing countries the employment and the profits which should be retained by Canadian labour and Canadian investment. It sends our expert workmen out of the country to obtain employment. It ruthlessly destroys the capital invested in those industries. It paralyzes the home industry, renders thousands of our people homeless, causes the abandonment of our towns and villages, and the destruction of civic life and property. It is burning down the house to cook the pig. It is absolutely essential for the well-being of this country that the government should devise other ways and means for preventing profiteering. I am convinced that on the part of 90 per cent of our industrial establishments there is no profiteering, and if there is profiteering among the other 10 per cent, then it is the duty of the government to devise other ways and means of defeating the profiteer than by destroying the town and village life in the places where such industry is conducted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What means would the
hon. gentleman take?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I made a suggestion to
the House the other day, that where a company was found upon examination to be profiteering there should be immediately imposed upon it an excise or a business tax which would render it impossible for that company to make a larger profit than might be considered reasonable.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a matter of appreciation, is it not?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It always is a matter of
appreciation. Now hon. gentlemen refer to the case of Mr. Ford. They say that from an original investment of $125,000 or thereabouts his company has now a capital of some $6,000,000 representing assets of between $8,000,000 and $9,000 000, bringing in a profit of $6,000,000 annually. I think that, in round figures, that is their contention.
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

What disadvantage would it be to Mr. Ford to remove the tariff on automobiles? Why, the removal of the tariff is the very thing which Mr. Ford and his associates are anxious to obtain, for tariff removal would enable them, by increasing their production in the American factories by five per cent, to supply all the requirements of Canada for Ford automobiles annually at any price that Mr. Ford might be prepared to fix. There may be a reduction in the price of automobiles, because a number of dealers have automobiles on hand, which, as a matter of fact, they are advertising at lower rates in order to get rid of them. But while I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet I venture to suggest that within a year American factories will be supplying these same automobiles to the Canadian consumer at relatively higher prices than they are now supplied by Canadian factories. Furthermore, I have not seen any statistics-although I have tried to read them all and examine them fairly-which indicate that any other factory than thie Ford has been making an undue profit out of the automobile industry in Canada.
An lion. MEMBER:	That is due to organization.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but it is due as well
to patents and a thousand other things. It is due chiefly to the fact that Mr. Ford controls a market in the United States of 110,000,000 which he is supplying with 2,000,000 cars of a standard size every year. In addition to that he has the advantages of mass production, so that he can undersell any competitor or raise or lower his price as he sees fit. But if the Canadian government were to impose a proper excise tax upon the Ford company in this country it would stop the profiteering complained of. I would impose such a tax as would prevent that $6.000 000 from reaching the pockets of Henry Ford. I would put on such a business tax as would make it unprofitable for him to charge the consumers of this country a price higher than would yield him a reasonable profit.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member wish to return to the business profits tax?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have a business profits
tax in this country at present. Whether we might amend that provision or levy a special excise tax I am not suggesting at the moment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A tax based on profits.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Based on undue profits. I
would take away the extravagant profits from industrial concerns which make use of the

Canadian tariff for the purposes of profiteering. I would discharge my public duty to the consumers of Canada by thus dealing with the ten per cent or five per cent of the factories that make that improper use of our tariff. We are, I believe, sufficiently intelligent in this country to devise ways and means of preventing profiteering to any undue extent, and certainly we can devise means of limiting the profits of a company such as the Ford.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The moment we applied any such excise tax, does the hon. member not think that we should hear a wail from certain towns and villages in which these concerns were situated to the effect that we were putting them out of business?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Possibly, but I am not dealing with wails of that kind.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What have you been doing
all evening?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a fair retort,
although I think it is a discourteous one. However, I accept it as courteous.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry if the hon. member thinks it was otherwise.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are living in proximity
to the United States and for years we have been endeavouring, Liberal governments as well as Conservative, to induce large producing manufacturing industries across the border to come into Canada and establish branch factories here. They have come in and given employment to thousands and tens of thousands of our people; new towns have been built up; new municipalities and cities have been established with all the various forms of municipal and civic life. Now we find one man profiteering unduly, and the only remedy that the Minister of Finance can suggest is to reduce quite materially the tariff which safeguards that industry. If carried to its logical conclusion that tariff reduction will result in the destruction of the automobile industry in this country, enabling the parent Ford industry in the United States to supply all its products to this country at prices which Mr. Ford may choose to fix.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am interested to know how my hon. friend arrives at the conclusion that interference with the tariff here will affect the fixation of prices in the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am dealing with the Ford Company, which is charged with undue profiteering. Mr. Henry Ford can fix prices in Canada just as he sees fit if the tariff is removed.

The Budget-Mr. Cahan

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why should the tariff have any influence on the fixation of his prices either up or down on the American side? I am referring to the American prices.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen have said
that allowing for the extra sales tax and for the fact that every man in this country pays 25 per cent of his entire income from productive activities to the federal, provincial and municipal governments by way of taxation-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I take issue with the hon. member on that point. However, that is not what I am getting at. How does my hon. friend argue that our interference with the tariff can affect prices in the United States?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen are saying
that, making allowance for everything in his favour, Mr. Ford is profiteering and charging an unreasonable price for his automobiles manufactured in Canada. You meet that by reducing the tariff. I say that has certain disadvantages to this country which I have enumerated, such as lack of employment and the transferring to the United States of the manufacture of the Ford car. Hon. gentlemen may laugh-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am laughing because that is not an answer to the question I asked my hon. friend. I am interested in his argument that the lowering of the tariff would permit Henry Ford and other American motor manufacturers to fix whatever prices suited them. I want to know what particular effect the tariff would have on the price of the car manufactured in the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Either I am very stupid
or the hon. minister is not stating his case very clearly. I do not say that it has any effect upon the price at which the car can be manufactured in the United States; but Henry Ford can fix any price he likes, either in the United States or Canada, his company will manufacture the car in the future in the United States, possibly assembling the parts in Canada, and he will fix the price in Canada within any reasonable limit that he sees fit.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
suggest that the Canadian price will be greater than the American price? If so, why?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know, but I say
Henry Ford has it entirely in his hands to fix the price.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What did the Belgians do
in the matter of glass?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a dozen such cases
before me if it were necessary to go into them, but I will take only one. Before the war Germany was producing dyes and selling them in the United States at certain prices per pound. The United States put up a tariff and thereby encouraged the domestic manufacture of dyes. The Germans thereupon lowered their price to such a level that it enabled them to overcome the American tariff and destroy the American dye factories. As soon as that was done they not only raised their price to the old level but added a fraction to make up for the profits they had lost while the American factories were functioning Take any similar case and you will find it so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
suggest that the American manufacturers would demand a greater price from Canadians than from their own people?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not the facts, but I have from as trustworthy authority as that of hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to many of the statements they made about the Ford car that the Ford company does discriminate sometimes as between different cities and districts. Naturally, you say, cost of transportation may account for this, but I believe there is that discrimination. And if you take down the tariff I can see no reason why, so far as the Ford car is concerned, the price should not be fixed in Canada at any figure Henry Ford sees fit to demand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Cannot we apply the hon.
gentleman's business tax in that case?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not see how you could. Mr. POWER: Apply the sales tax here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then you would pay it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You would pay it, anyway.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now, my suggestion is that we should not admit we are so wanting in intelligence as not to be able to devise ways and means for putting an end to profiteering without burning down our industrial establishments.
As it is nearing eleven o'clock and I wisn to conclude, let me say I regard it as absolutely necessary for the proper development of our industrial life that we should have a wise and vigorous government policy that persists in the single aim, year in and year out, through one administration after the other, no matter what political party may command a majority in this House-the single aim of maintaining a stable tariff which is not subject to sudden change for the pur-

The Budget-Mr. Cahan

pose of helping the friends of one political party or of injuring the friends of another political party; a policy which is not subject to change except after due inquiry and careful consideration and a report to the government and to this House in justification of the change proposed. The changes which have been made under present conditions have unsettled the whole country. Gentlemen opposite may smile and think they are proposing something which is accepted generally from one end of the country to the other. That is not so. The cheerful smile which pervaded their countenances on the day the Minister of Finance announced his budget has entirely disappeared-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not from these faces.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the various speeches on the budget it would almost appear that there was nothing further to be said, but every hon. member seems to be able to rarse something new. I intend for a few minutes to speak in the hope that I may be able to disabuse the minds of some hon. gentlemen of the wrong impressions that have been conveyed to them.
Let me say, though, that I have no doubt hon. members on both sides of the House are anxious only to assist in legislation that will be in the interests of Canada as a whole. We cannot all see things alike, and we are all prone to take a different view of the same set of facts. But we do hope that a thorough discussion of any subject may enable us to arrive at a conclusion that will give us a proper solution of our difficulties. We are somewhat prone to stress the importance of our own constituency or our own province, but I think we all realize that no matter what part of Canada we come from we all belong to this great Dominion and must assist m legislation which is in the interests of the country as a whole.

It must be a matter of congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb)-indeed, to everyone-to see that we are at last emerging to some degree from the clouds of debt with which we have been surrounded. We know the Great war entailed a tremendous expense, and that we had to assume tremendous obligations after the war during the period of reconstruction. An enormous debt was then piled up, and it is now our duty to see that debt liquidated. Our favourable position, as announced by the Minister of Finance in his budget address, is to no small extent resultant from the bounteous crops with which we have been favoured for the past two years, but our bounteous harvests are not sufficient without other means by which use can be made of them. The Minister of Finance was able to announce that Canada's favourable financial position is due in part to the trade treaties into which Canada has entered. Those treaties, together with the wonderful harvests, have enabled us to bring forward the budget which was presented the other day.
Since this session opened I have at times been alarmed by the statements made from opposition benches as to the dire straits in which Canada found itself. During the early days of the session particularly, we were almost convinced that we were on the verge of bankruptcy; from what various hon. members opposite said we might almost have thought our own conclusions wrong. We had been led to believe that Canada was in a fairly prosperous position, judging from newspaper reports, statements of financial institutions, market reports of various kinds and agricultural conditions generally. Imagine then, how we looked on the situation when we heard what hon. members had to say in this House. We were also surprised to learn, coming from a province which has been developing its dairy industry, that the dairy and poultry industries were being destroyed by the Australian treaty; we could scarcely believe it. I believe that suggestion has been dissipated by the speeches since made in this House, and I do not intend to deal with that question. We were also surprised to learn, from the speeches of hon. members opposite, that there was no legislative programme in favour of the farmers of Canada; now we hear that the legislative programme is all in favour of the farmers of western Canada.
The Speech from the Throne held out hopes of a legislative programme in the in terests of Canada from shore to shore. It is true that Maritime conditions were such as to make it a difficult matter for any government to bring down legislation which would satisfy the people of the Maritimes. I have listene 1

The Budget-Mr. Bothwell
to the speeches in this House dealing with Maritime rights, and I must confess that I do not yet know definitely just what Maritime rights are, nor do I know what legislation the Maritime righters require in order to have their claims satisfied. We are told of promises made when the Maritime provinces entered confederation; those promises, . so far as I know, have been fulfilled. Then we are told of understandings reached between various parts of Canada at that time, and judging from some of the speeches there were some such understandings. If it is possible for the people of Canada to carry out not only those promises but the understandings as well, that should be done, but I believe we will know '' at those understandings and rights are **' ugii the commission appointed to inquire into this question. Surely that commission can bring recommendations to this House which will result in legislation to relieve, to some extent at all events, the people of the Maritimes.
It is claimed that immediate steps should be taken to encourage and foster the coal industry in the Maritimes. We expect the commission to go into that question and make recommendations, but I do not know whether the claims made for the Maritimes would be permanent solution of those difficulties. I hardly know whether sufficient stress has been placed on the condition of the coal industry, not only in the Maritimes but throughout the world.

There is a difference, as I see it. In spite of the quotations and citations made in this House to show that the rates on shipments of western grain to 14011-194.J
the east occasion a loss to the railways, I believe-and in fact we know-that when great shipments of grain are moving east the railways are making their big profits, and I believe the grain coming from western Canada pays its way and leaves a reasonable return to the railways. If that commission finds, in studying Maritime conditions, that the freight rates from the Maritimes to central Canada should be reduced, I would say they should be reduced, and I believe there are two commissions inquiring into that matter at present.
I was speaking of the coal industry in Nova Scotia and the changing world conditions so far as coal is concerned. From the Daily Mail Year Book of 1926 I take the following statement, made by F. H. Rose, member of parliament for Aberdeen. He says:
It is difficult (to conceive a more serious and thought-compelling prospect for a great industrial nation, than the chronic decline in one of its major activities and this we have to face and deal with. The facts are clear enough. Before the war, unemployment in the sense that it now exists was an unknown element in colliery work. Men were temporarily out of work through defects in their working places, odd individuals were employed for various personal reasons, but a mass of colliers without employers and without jobs was unknown. To-day there must be at least as many chronically unemployed as shown in the table appended.
I will not read the table. He goes on to say:
It is not without serious thought that I submit the proposition that the coal trade is declining, and it will continue to decline as years go on, until it ceases to be major industry-here and elsewhere in the world. For the phenomena of a current transition are apparent all over the world. The rapid development of the motorship and the motor tractor are not entirely accountable for the conditions. The use of hydro-electricity by Italy and the Scandinavian nations has closed or is closing our middle coal markets (our distant markets were never very important). Our iron and steel manufactures are steadily passing from coke to electricity and their processes. Every effort of the modern scientist and inventor is directed now to economizing coal and the production of cheaper and cleaner and vastly more effective agencies for raising power, light and heat.
The effect of these innovations bears so heavily upon the industrial and social life of our people that an industrial writer may well be excused for emphasizing it. No reflective person can avoid the inevitable implications which arise from its consideration and the simple fact is that the world is using less coal to-day than it used yesterday and will be using less to-morrow than to-day. It is superfluous to stress the importance to our nation of a declining industry or its bearing upon the questions of unemployment and our social life.
Now, just what the situation is in the Maritimes so far as the coal industry is 'concerned, having regard to that portion of Mr. Rose's address which I have read, I do not know, but I am prepared to say,-and I believe I am speaking for western members generally when I make the statement-that

In addition to the eoial industry there is the iron and steel industry in the Maritime provinces, and in this connection I have been much interested in reading the publication known as the Besco Bulletin. I have endeavoured by a study of that publication to find out, to some extent, what the trouble is in the Maritimes. I find from the issue of April 24th that they have four serious disappointments in the budget. They are as follows:
No. 1. Failure to adjust the specific duties on the basic forms of iron and steed so as to bring their ad valorem effect up to the general level of duties on other matenials.
No. 2. Failure to correct the mistake made last year when the duty on bituminous coal was Lowered three cents instead of being raised, and failure to make anthracite screenings dutiable at the same rate as soft coal with which it competes.
No. 3. Failure 'to take up the matter of dealing effectively with the importation of materials produced in countries whose currency is greatly depreciated, which was dropped in a moment of weakness last session, and which is now of greater urgency than it was a year ago.
No. 4. Persistent adherence to the pernicious policy of encouraging the [DOT]importation of finished goods by lowering the duties, and of partly finished materials by refunding the duties specified in the customs tariff.
"Disappointment No. 2," dealing with the duty on bituminous coal, has to do with the very question which was raised by my hon. friend optposite a short time ago. That is one of the "disappointments", apparently, in so far as Besco is concerned, that we hope to have remedied through the commission on Maritime rights.

I want to touch for a moment or two on the question of the tariff on automobiles. I think every member who has spoken on the budget has dealt with this subject. We have had deputations appear here and the matter has been presented in various ways from both sides of the House. The same question was before the House last year, and I notice that after the debate in the House a year ago the resolution was defeated by only nineteen votes. That would appear to me to be a pretty fair intimation to the automobile manufacturers in Canada that some legislation would be passed this session. Further than that, I think practically every newspaper in Canada has carried requests for months past in connection with the reduction in the tariff on automobiles. During the darly days of this session a resolution by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) was placed on the order paper, showing that he intended to ask for a reduction of the duty on automobiles. We know too that a good deal of lobbying was being done around this House by the automobile interests and speeches of various kinds were, made in this House in the interest of the automobile industry. It strikes me as most peculiar that if it is necessary that the automobile tariff should remain where -it was, no single individual either in this House or in the lobby or anywhere else seems to be able to give us a concrete instance of any industry that would suffer by a reduction in the tariff if it were made. So far as I have been able to find out, no single concrete case has been put ou record to show that any factory, whether having to do with parts or automobiles, would have to close its doors by reason of a change in the tariff. Surely if the experts that have been able to get out books such as we have received from the automobile industry knew that a reduction in the tariff was going to ruin their industry, they would have been able to give us manufacturing costs and facts showing that such a reduction could not safely be made.
But it has been left for Mr. Ford to make his statement that it is quite in order to bring about the reduction, and that statement has not been met by any other manufacturer in Canada so far as I have been able to gather.
I presume every hon. member has received a copy of the book that has been got out by the Ford interests, because we have had it quoted at different times. It would appear from that book that the people of Canada have given the automobile manufacturers fairly good protection. Mr. Ford in the interview that was put on Hansard by the hon.
[Mr Bothwell.]
member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) stated that in his plant in Canada they use at least S5 per cent of Canadian material. He says in this book of his, and also in the interview that was read by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that the cost of manufacture is about equally divided between wages and material; that is, that wages and material cost about the same. This book of his says that wages paid out in 1925 amounted to $10,138,927. Eighty-five per cent of his product is procured in Canada. If he takes the 15 per cent from the United States, that would mean on his own figures that he would bring in approximately $1,520,838. His production cost, according to the same book on page 6, is given as $19,329,745, being spent for production material, building construction, machinery equipment, supplies, insurance, advertising and other services. He has the money bags appear at the bottom of the picture showing that the company pay to the government $2,962,234.

How Canadian Company Started "Did you establish your plant in Canada because of the tariff?" "No. I didn't establish it at all. It happened this way. Mr. McGregor (referring to the late vice-.president and general manager of the Ford Company of Canada) was running a buggy works over at Windsor. "I'd never seen him before but I liked his looks and said:	'AH right, I'm interested in that sort of
thing. Three months later McGregor opened the plant.

I never thought anything about the tariff. I never have in starting a plant."
"What about Manchester?" I asked. "I started the plant in Manchester," said Mr. Ford, "to put industry into the country. Tariff had nothing to do with it. All our plants have been located to serve *different localities, like the twenty or more we have in the United States. I would want to manufacture in Canada for the same reason,"
"And you believe the tariff is not a factor in locating .in Canada" "It is not with me," replied Mr. Ford.	*	.	.
Mr. Ford was silent .for a moment, thinking. The stockholder," he said at last, "is the only person who may lose in the tariff reduction, and he's had enough anyway. We shouldn't worry about stockholders. They don't deserve profits; they don't earn."
